title: Medication review before conception
stem: A client whose epilepsy is controlled with prescribed medication hopes to conceive in three months. They ask what to do about possible fetal medication effects. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue the current plan until a preconception medication review is arranged
Reduce medication only during the first trimester
Wait for a positive pregnancy test before requesting advice
Substitute a nonprescription supplement while awaiting assessment
why: Planned review balances fetal exposure concerns against seizure-control needs without abrupt treatment changes.
Unsupervised dose reduction can cause breakthrough seizures and does not establish fetal safety.
Waiting loses an opportunity to optimize treatment before early fetal development.
A supplement does not provide established antiseizure treatment or assured pregnancy safety.
takeaway: Arrange preconception medication review while maintaining prescribed therapy pending advice.
learningObjective: Arrange preconception medication review while maintaining prescribed therapy pending advice.

title: Workplace exposure assessment
stem: A client planning pregnancy works in a laboratory and asks whether to request reassignment. They feel well and cannot name the chemicals handled. What should the nurse do first?
options: Recommend avoiding all laboratory duties immediately
Obtain substance and exposure information for occupational-health review
Recommend changing to an evening shift while awaiting advice
Base advice on coworkers' uncomplicated pregnancies
why: Blanket reassignment precedes assessment of the actual exposure and available controls.
Specific substances, routes and protections are needed for a meaningful occupational assessment.
Changing shifts does not establish or control substance-specific exposure.
Other workers' outcomes do not establish this client's exposure level or risk.
takeaway: Characterize workplace exposures before recommending individualized pregnancy precautions.
learningObjective: Characterize workplace exposures before recommending individualized pregnancy precautions.

title: Discussing an early alcohol exposure
stem: At the first prenatal visit, a client reports drinking before recognizing pregnancy and asks whether anything can still help. Which response best supports health promotion?
options: Focus on whether ultrasound can exclude all effects
Explain that avoiding further alcohol and continuing prenatal care remain useful
Recommend reducing intake gradually without further assessment
Defer the topic until the client can recall every drink
why: Ultrasound cannot exclude every possible effect and does not address preventable ongoing exposure.
Nonjudgmental advice supports prevention and care without predicting an individual fetal outcome.
A reduction plan requires assessment; the safest pregnancy recommendation is to avoid alcohol.
Incomplete recall should not delay supportive assessment and prevention advice.
takeaway: Support abstinence and prenatal follow-up without making unsupported predictions about past exposure.
learningObjective: Support abstinence and prenatal follow-up without making unsupported predictions about past exposure.

title: Planning a vegan prenatal diet
stem: A pregnant vegan client eats beans, grains, vegetables and fruit but takes no supplements. Weight gain is appropriate. Which assessment is most useful next?
options: Whether a higher calorie target is needed solely because the diet is vegan
Whether meat can be added before further counselling
Sources of vitamin B12, iron and other required prenatal nutrients
Whether normal weight gain removes the need for nutritional review
why: Calorie adequacy and micronutrient adequacy are different questions in this scenario.
A nutritionally adequate plan may be developed within the client's dietary preferences.
Appropriate weight gain does not establish adequate intake of B12 or other nutrients.
Weight gain alone cannot rule out a nutrient gap.
takeaway: Assess specific nutrient sources even when prenatal weight gain appears appropriate.
learningObjective: Assess specific nutrient sources even when prenatal weight gain appears appropriate.

title: Pregnancy nausea with preserved intake
stem: At ten weeks, a client reports morning nausea, stable weight and retained fluids. Which teaching is appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Try small meals more frequently
Identify and avoid personal food triggers
Report inability to retain fluids
Drink most fluids together with meals
why: Smaller portions may be more tolerable without unnecessarily restricting overall intake.
Trigger identification allows an individualized rather than blanket dietary adjustment.
Loss of fluid tolerance changes the need for clinical assessment.
Separating fluids from meals may improve tolerance; large combined volumes can worsen nausea.
takeaway: Pair practical nausea strategies with clear advice about worsening intake.
learningObjective: Pair practical nausea strategies with clear advice about worsening intake.

title: Prenatal food insecurity
stem: A pregnant client understands the meal plan but skips lunch to preserve food for their children. What nursing response best addresses the identified barrier?
options: Repeat teaching about fetal nutrient requirements
Set a goal to document every missed meal
Offer referral to accessible food and income supports
Ask the client to purchase smaller prenatal supplement packages
why: The client already understands the advice; limited resources prevent using it.
Tracking alone does not make food available to the household.
Material supports address the stated barrier to adequate intake.
Supplements cannot replace meals, and smaller packages may not improve affordability.
takeaway: Match prenatal interventions to resource barriers rather than assuming a knowledge deficit.
learningObjective: Match prenatal interventions to resource barriers rather than assuming a knowledge deficit.

title: Continuing prenatal activity
stem: A client who walks regularly has an uncomplicated pregnancy and no activity restrictions. They ask how to adapt activity as pregnancy progresses. Which advice is best?
options: Maintain exactly the same distance regardless of symptoms
Stop structured activity and rely only on household tasks
Switch to an unfamiliar intensive exercise program
Adjust activity to comfort and discuss new warning symptoms promptly
why: A fixed distance ignores changing tolerance and emerging clinical concerns.
Uncomplicated pregnancy does not by itself require stopping enjoyable activity.
Unfamiliar intensive training needs assessment rather than routine recommendation.
Individual adaptation supports activity while preserving responsiveness to warning signs.
takeaway: Adapt prenatal activity to tolerance and clinical status.
learningObjective: Adapt prenatal activity to tolerance and clinical status.

title: A symptom during prenatal exercise
stem: During a low-intensity prenatal class, a client reports new vaginal bleeding. They are alert and deny pain. What should the nurse advise first?
options: Stop activity and contact the maternity service promptly
Rest briefly and resume if bleeding stops
Change to seated exercise for the remainder of class
Record the episode for the next routine prenatal visit
why: Bleeding requires timely assessment even without pain or altered consciousness.
Temporary improvement does not establish that continuing exercise is appropriate.
Changing exercise type does not evaluate the cause of bleeding.
A routine future visit may delay needed assessment.
takeaway: Stop prenatal exercise and seek assessment for vaginal bleeding.
learningObjective: Stop prenatal exercise and seek assessment for vaginal bleeding.

title: Dental assessment during pregnancy
stem: A pregnant client has gum bleeding when brushing and has postponed a routine dental visit. Which teaching best addresses the concern?
options: Continue hygiene and arrange an oral-health assessment now
Stop flossing until the postpartum visit
Use mouthwash instead of brushing until bleeding resolves
Increase calcium intake before deciding whether dental care is needed
why: Ongoing hygiene and assessment address oral disease without unnecessary pregnancy-related delay.
Stopping cleaning may worsen plaque-related inflammation.
Mouthwash does not replace mechanical plaque removal or clinical assessment.
Nutrient changes do not identify the cause of gum bleeding.
takeaway: Encourage oral assessment and effective hygiene during pregnancy.
learningObjective: Encourage oral assessment and effective hygiene during pregnancy.

title: Reviewing vaccines before birth
stem: A client says, 'I had my vaccines years ago, so pregnancy should not change anything.' Which review elements are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Document previous doses and reactions
Check current pregnancy-specific recommendations
Explain potential protection of the newborn
Apply the routine adult schedule without checking pregnancy precautions
why: Previous doses and reactions inform what is indicated and safe.
Some recommendations depend specifically on pregnancy and gestational timing.
Maternal immunization can provide protection during early infancy.
Pregnancy may alter vaccine selection and timing, so adult guidance alone is insufficient.
takeaway: Use pregnancy-specific Canadian guidance alongside the client's vaccine history.
learningObjective: Use pregnancy-specific Canadian guidance alongside the client's vaccine history.

title: Sexual health during pregnancy
stem: A pregnant client has a new partner and asks whether condoms are unnecessary now. What is the best response?
options: Discuss condom use and appropriate sexually transmitted infection assessment
Focus only on postpartum contraception
Recommend relying on a partner's lack of symptoms
Delay infection screening until after delivery unless symptoms develop
why: Pregnancy prevents neither exposure nor infection, and screening may be indicated without symptoms.
Future contraception does not address current infection exposure.
Several sexually transmitted infections can be asymptomatic.
Delayed assessment may miss opportunities to protect the client and infant.
takeaway: Include infection prevention and risk-based screening in prenatal sexual-health teaching.
learningObjective: Include infection prevention and risk-based screening in prenatal sexual-health teaching.

title: Preparing for changing birth circumstances
stem: A client strongly prefers a particular labour plan and worries that staff will disregard it. Which nursing response best supports informed preparation?
options: Explain that written preferences remove the need for further consent discussions
Explore priorities and how options will be discussed if circumstances change
Suggest omitting preferences to avoid disappointment
Focus only on the standard unit routine
why: Preferences guide care but do not replace ongoing information and consent.
Understanding priorities supports meaningful shared decisions when the clinical situation evolves.
Avoiding preferences removes useful information about what matters to the client.
Routine information alone does not address the client's concern about participation.
takeaway: Discuss both birth priorities and communication when care options change.
learningObjective: Discuss both birth priorities and communication when care options change.

title: A change in fetal activity
stem: At 33 weeks, a client reports substantially less fetal movement than usual this afternoon. They have no bleeding or pain. What advice is most appropriate?
options: Reassess at tomorrow's usual active time
Bring the concern to the next routine appointment
Contact the maternity service promptly for individualized assessment
Drink something cold and call only if movement has not increased by bedtime
why: Waiting until tomorrow may delay evaluation of a meaningful change.
Absence of pain does not make delayed review sufficient.
A reduction from the established pattern warrants prompt maternity advice and assessment.
Attempts to stimulate movement should not postpone contact for a meaningful change.
takeaway: Act promptly on a meaningful reduction in the usual fetal movement pattern.
learningObjective: Act promptly on a meaningful reduction in the usual fetal movement pattern.

title: Planning a labour support role
stem: A client asks a close friend to support them during birth. The friend feels uncertain about helping. Which preparation is most useful?
options: Practise a fixed breathing schedule before asking about preferences
Ask the friend to select all pain-relief options in advance
Give only the hospital visiting policy
Discuss the client's preferences and practise agreed comfort measures
why: Comfort methods should be adapted to the client rather than fixed in advance.
A support person does not replace the capable client's ongoing decisions.
Visiting information alone does not prepare the friend to provide support.
Shared expectations and practical rehearsal make support responsive to the client.
takeaway: Prepare labour support around the client's preferences and practical comfort needs.
learningObjective: Prepare labour support around the client's preferences and practical comfort needs.

title: Planning accessible prenatal care
stem: A client misses prenatal visits because shifts change weekly and bus service is limited. Which actions address the barriers? Select all that apply.
options: Explore feasible appointment times
Ask about transport assistance
Discuss which follow-up components can safely occur remotely
Offer video visits for all remaining appointments
why: Scheduling flexibility can reduce the identified employment conflict.
Transport assistance addresses a concrete access problem.
Appropriate remote components may improve access while preserving necessary in-person assessment.
Universal remote substitution can miss necessary examinations or tests.
takeaway: Reduce practical barriers when arranging prenatal follow-up.
learningObjective: Reduce practical barriers when arranging prenatal follow-up.

title: Cannabis used for pregnancy nausea
stem: A client uses cannabis edibles for nausea and believes avoiding smoke eliminates pregnancy risks. Which response is most accurate?
options: Edibles are preferred throughout pregnancy because there is no smoke
Cannabis exposure remains; arrange review of safer nausea treatments
Stop all nausea treatments until the next trimester
Use symptom relief as evidence that the product is safe
why: Avoiding smoke does not eliminate exposure to cannabis constituents.
Route changes do not establish fetal safety, and nausea deserves an assessed treatment plan.
Untreated nausea may compromise intake; options can be reviewed now.
A product can relieve symptoms without being appropriate during pregnancy.
takeaway: Explain that edible cannabis does not remove pregnancy exposure concerns.
learningObjective: Explain that edible cannabis does not remove pregnancy exposure concerns.

title: Postpartum practical supports
stem: A client expecting a first baby lives alone and has no nearby family. Which question best guides a useful support plan?
options: Which infant-care techniques would you like demonstrated before discharge?
Would you prefer a telephone check-in at the end of the first week?
'Which daily tasks may be difficult, and who or what services could help?'
'Would reading another parenting booklet settle your concern?'
why: Skill teaching may help but does not first identify the practical support gap.
Follow-up is useful but does not first establish help with daily tasks.
Task-specific assessment identifies feasible help with meals, rest and infant care.
More information alone may not resolve a lack of practical assistance.
takeaway: Assess practical postpartum needs and available supports before birth.
learningObjective: Assess practical postpartum needs and available supports before birth.

title: Rubella protection before conception
stem: A client is not pregnant, plans conception soon and has documented lack of rubella immunity. What should the nurse arrange?
options: Vaccine counselling that includes waiting at least four weeks before conception
Deferring vaccination until after the planned pregnancy
Vaccination without discussing a conception interval
Repeating serology after conception before counselling
why: Canadian guidance recommends delaying conception at least four weeks after rubella-containing vaccination.
A susceptible nonpregnant client can consider protection before conception.
Timing advice is part of safe preconception vaccine counselling.
Waiting loses an opportunity to plan protection before pregnancy.
takeaway: Review rubella vaccination and conception timing before pregnancy.
learningObjective: Review rubella vaccination and conception timing before pregnancy.

title: Health literacy in prenatal information
stem: A client shows two conflicting prenatal supplement advertisements and asks which claim to trust. Which approach best supports independent information appraisal?
options: Choose the advertisement with more testimonials
Compare authorship, evidence, date and relevance with a trusted clinical source
Select the product described as natural
Use the more expensive product as the quality standard
why: Testimonials cannot establish effectiveness or safety for this client.
Source appraisal helps distinguish evidence from marketing and supports future decisions.
Natural origin does not establish supplement safety.
Price is not a reliable measure of clinical evidence.
takeaway: Teach source appraisal when prenatal information is commercially promoted.
learningObjective: Teach source appraisal when prenatal information is commercially promoted.

title: Postpartum follow-up planning
stem: A client will have help overnight for three days after birth but is unsure who will review their feeding concerns after discharge. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm how and when feeding follow-up will occur
Agree on rest opportunities during the available support
Assume the routine later postpartum visit covers every early feeding concern
Arrange an additional support option when the initial help ends
why: A clear follow-up route supports timely assessment of feeding difficulties.
Matching rest to actual available help makes the plan feasible.
New feeding concerns may need earlier assessment than a routine later visit.
Anticipating the end of current support prevents an avoidable gap.
takeaway: Coordinate postpartum support with actual availability and follow-up needs.
learningObjective: Coordinate postpartum support with actual availability and follow-up needs.

title: Observing breastfeeding discomfort
stem: During a home visit, a parent reports pinching pain throughout breastfeeds. The infant feeds frequently but often slips off. What should the nurse do first?
options: Shorten every feed to reduce nipple exposure
Observe a full feed and assess attachment and milk transfer
Recommend a fixed four-hour feeding schedule
Suggest pumping exclusively before observing feeding
why: Shortening feeds may reduce intake without correcting the underlying problem.
Pain and slipping suggest a correctable feeding issue that direct observation can clarify.
Restricting frequency does not address ineffective attachment.
A major feeding change is premature before assessing the parent's chosen method.
takeaway: Observe latch and milk transfer when feeding is painful or ineffective.
learningObjective: Observe latch and milk transfer when feeding is painful or ineffective.

title: Evidence of milk transfer
stem: During a breastfeed, an infant remains attached for 30 minutes. Which additional observation most directly supports effective milk transfer?
options: The parent reports fuller breasts before feeding
The infant's eyes remain closed
Rhythmic sucking followed by audible swallowing
The infant sucks rapidly throughout the feed without observed swallowing
why: Breast fullness alone does not show what the infant receives.
Closed eyes do not establish effective intake.
Swallowing linked to sucking is direct evidence of milk transfer.
Rapid sucking without swallowing does not establish effective milk transfer.
takeaway: Assess swallowing rather than feed duration alone when evaluating milk transfer.
learningObjective: Assess swallowing rather than feed duration alone when evaluating milk transfer.

title: Responsive bottle feeding
stem: A caregiver reports repeatedly encouraging a well-growing infant to finish bottles despite turning away. Which teaching is most appropriate?
options: Pause or stop when the infant shows fullness cues
Prepare a larger bottle to reduce feeding frequency
Increase flow so feeding finishes before the infant turns away
Schedule feeds solely by the printed age guide
why: Responsive feeding respects fullness and avoids pressuring intake beyond cues.
Larger bottles may reinforce the same pressure to finish.
Faster flow can overwhelm coordination and does not address satiety.
Age guides do not replace the individual infant's hunger and fullness signals.
takeaway: Use hunger and satiety cues to guide bottle feeding.
learningObjective: Use hunger and satiety cues to guide bottle feeding.

title: Formula affordability and preparation
stem: A caregiver dilutes formula to make a container last longer. The infant has no current symptoms. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Change to a more concentrated homemade mixture
Advise smaller feeds without discussing preparation
Wait for the next growth check before intervening
Review correct preparation and connect the family with formula-access support
why: An improvised mixture cannot ensure safe nutrient or electrolyte content.
Smaller feeds do not correct inappropriate concentration or food insecurity.
Preparation errors warrant intervention before symptoms appear.
Correct preparation addresses immediate safety while resource support addresses the cause.
takeaway: Address both unsafe formula dilution and the financial barrier driving it.
learningObjective: Address both unsafe formula dilution and the financial barrier driving it.

title: Synthesizing newborn intake findings
stem: At a day-eight visit, a newborn continues to lose weight, has fewer wet diapers than two days ago and rarely swallows during long feeds. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Reassure the parent because frequent long feeds indicate adequate intake
Arrange prompt feeding and clinical assessment
Shorten feeds and review growth at the next routine visit
Increase intervals between feeds to strengthen hunger cues
why: Feeding duration does not outweigh the concerning weight, output and transfer pattern.
The combined findings suggest inadequate intake requiring timely assessment and a feeding plan.
Waiting without addressing falling weight and reduced output may delay necessary support.
Longer gaps can further reduce intake and do not correct ineffective transfer.
takeaway: Integrate weight, output and observed transfer when deciding whether newborn intake needs assessment.
learningObjective: Integrate weight, output and observed transfer when deciding whether newborn intake needs assessment.

title: Complementary food selection
stem: A six-month-old sits with support, controls their head and shows interest in food. Which first-food plan best addresses emerging nutritional needs?
options: Fruit juice between milk feeds
Iron-rich soft foods alongside milk feeds
Low-fat milk replacing breastfeeds
Vegetable broth replacing one daily feed
why: Juice supplies little iron and can displace nutritious intake.
Suitable iron-rich foods complement continuing milk nutrition.
Low-fat milk is not an appropriate replacement here.
Broth alone provides inadequate complementary nutrition.
takeaway: Include iron-rich foods when complementary feeding begins.
learningObjective: Include iron-rich foods when complementary feeding begins.

title: Advancing feeding skills
stem: A nine-month-old handles mashed foods comfortably but receives only smooth purées because they lack molars. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Continue smooth foods until molars erupt
Add cereal to every bottle
Introduce suitable soft finger foods under supervision
Delay self-feeding until spoon use is precise
why: Suitable texture progression need not wait for molars.
Bottle cereal does not develop texture-handling skills.
Soft foods allow developmentally appropriate chewing and self-feeding practice.
Waiting for precision removes opportunities to learn.
takeaway: Advance food texture according to feeding ability.
learningObjective: Advance food texture according to feeding ability.

title: Honey in infant food
stem: A caregiver offers homemade yogurt sweetened with honey to an eight-month-old. What ingredient change should the nurse prioritize?
options: Replace honey with suitable mashed fruit
Replace yogurt with fruit juice
Heat the honey at home before adding it
Use pasteurized honey in the recipe
why: Avoiding honey reduces infant botulism exposure during the first year.
Juice substitution does not address the specific honey risk.
Routine domestic heating does not reliably eliminate botulism spores.
Pasteurization does not reliably eliminate the relevant spores.
takeaway: Avoid honey before 12 months of age.
learningObjective: Avoid honey before 12 months of age.

title: Mealtime positioning
stem: A parent feeds an older infant soft pieces while the infant moves around the living room. What is the most useful change?
options: Offer only purées while moving
Give smaller portions but maintain the routine
Allow independent eating in a reclined stroller
Seat the infant upright and supervise the meal
why: Changing texture does not correct an unstable feeding position.
Portion size alone does not address movement-related risk.
Reclining does not support an optimal feeding position.
Stable upright supervised eating supports safer swallowing.
takeaway: Establish upright supervised meals for complementary feeding.
learningObjective: Establish upright supervised meals for complementary feeding.

title: Responsive infant feeding
stem: Which observations suggest a bottle-fed infant may be ready to pause or stop? Select all that apply.
options: Turning away repeatedly
Closing the mouth when offered the nipple
Relaxing after feeding without seeking more
Rooting actively toward the nipple
why: Turning away can communicate fullness or need for a break.
Closing the mouth indicates disengagement rather than permission to insist.
Relaxed satisfaction supports pausing and observing further cues.
Active rooting is more consistent with feeding interest.
takeaway: Recognize satiety cues instead of pressuring bottle completion.
learningObjective: Recognize satiety cues instead of pressuring bottle completion.

title: Coping with infant crying
stem: A tired parent says, 'I am getting so angry I need to put the baby down.' The infant appears well. What is the best immediate advice?
options: Continue holding until the crying ends
Place the infant safely in a crib and take a brief calming break
Leave the infant on a sofa within hearing distance
Begin a detailed feeding diary immediately
why: Continuing while overwhelmed may increase the risk of losing control.
Safe placement permits a brief pause and help-seeking.
A sofa is not a safe unattended infant surface.
Documentation is secondary to immediate caregiver regulation and infant safety.
takeaway: Use safe placement and a calming break when crying overwhelms caregivers.
learningObjective: Use safe placement and a calming break when crying overwhelms caregivers.

title: Infant language interaction
stem: A family speaks two languages and asks how to support early communication. Which activity is most useful?
options: Repeated vocabulary videos
Use only one family language until first words develop
Responsive talking and reading in familiar family languages
Practise naming the same pictures repeatedly
why: Passive media do not replace responsive interpersonal language learning.
Responsive multilingual interaction need not be restricted because several languages are used.
Responsive exchanges provide meaningful language and social experience.
Repeated labels offer less responsive interaction than exchanges that include the infant's gestures and interests.
takeaway: Encourage responsive communication in languages the family uses comfortably.
learningObjective: Encourage responsive communication in languages the family uses comfortably.

title: A new infant hearing concern
stem: A six-month-old who passed newborn hearing screening now persistently fails to turn toward familiar voices. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Arrange timely hearing and developmental assessment
Repeat observations at the next routine visit
Introduce louder interactive toys during play
Keep a monthly log of first words
why: A previous screen does not resolve a current persistent concern; reassessment can identify later or missed difficulty.
Routine observation alone can delay assessment of this established pattern.
Louder toys do not establish hearing ability or identify the cause.
Waiting for words may delay support for a hearing-related communication barrier.
takeaway: Reassess persistent hearing concerns despite a previous normal newborn screen.
learningObjective: Reassess persistent hearing concerns despite a previous normal newborn screen.

title: Loss of toddler skills
stem: A toddler previously used several words but now rarely speaks and no longer points. What is the best action?
options: Practise words for a month before arranging assessment
Attribute the change to a new sibling
Focus solely on increasing vocabulary practice
Arrange prompt developmental and hearing assessment
why: Home practice can accompany, but should not postpone, evaluation of regression.
A family change should not automatically explain developmental regression.
Regression across communication behaviours requires broader assessment.
Loss of learned skills warrants timely evaluation.
takeaway: Escalate developmental regression rather than reassuring from age alone.
learningObjective: Escalate developmental regression rather than reassuring from age alone.

title: Interpreting growth data
stem: Which information helps interpret an infant's unexpectedly low weight measurement? Select all that apply.
options: Previous measurements and trajectory
Measurement technique and equipment
Feeding history and current health
Whether the infant exceeds a sibling's weight at that age
why: Serial data distinguish a stable pattern from a concerning change.
Technique errors can create misleading apparent growth changes.
Intake and illness provide essential clinical context.
Sibling comparisons do not establish this infant's expected trajectory.
takeaway: Verify measurements and clinical context before interpreting growth change.
learningObjective: Verify measurements and clinical context before interpreting growth change.

title: Development after preterm birth
stem: A four-month-old infant was born eight weeks early. The parent worries because a term-born cousin has more advanced skills. What should guide the nurse's discussion?
options: The cousin's developmental pace
Corrected age and the infant's progress across domains
Birth weight as the sole comparison
The number of weeks spent in hospital
why: Another infant's pace is not an individualized developmental standard.
Corrected age contextualizes early expectations after prematurity.
Birth weight alone cannot determine developmental milestones.
Hospital duration does not replace developmental assessment.
takeaway: Use corrected age and longitudinal progress after premature birth.
learningObjective: Use corrected age and longitudinal progress after premature birth.

title: Stranger distress during assessment
stem: A nine-month-old cries when the nurse approaches but settles with their caregiver. A routine assessment is due. Which approach is best?
options: Complete the examination quickly despite distress
Separate the caregiver to reduce distraction
Begin gradually while the caregiver holds the infant
Postpone all assessments until stranger distress disappears
why: Rushing may intensify distress and reduce useful observations.
Removing familiar support can worsen developmental anxiety.
A familiar secure base improves tolerance of nonurgent assessment.
Care can usually proceed with developmentally appropriate adaptation.
takeaway: Adapt routine assessments to infant stranger anxiety.
learningObjective: Adapt routine assessments to infant stranger anxiety.

title: Chalky changes on primary teeth
stem: A parent reports white chalky areas near a toddler's gumline but no pain. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Arrange dental assessment before pain develops
Review only at the next annual physical
Increase brushing pressure to remove the marks
Wait until permanent teeth replace them
why: Early decay may be painless and benefit from timely treatment.
Delayed review may allow preventable progression.
Excess pressure can injure tissues and does not diagnose the change.
Primary teeth have important functions and warrant care.
takeaway: Refer early tooth changes even when pain is absent.
learningObjective: Refer early tooth changes even when pain is absent.

title: Toothbrushing independence
stem: A four-year-old insists on brushing alone but misses back teeth. Which plan best supports development and oral health?
options: Let the child manage independently to build confidence
Replace brushing with rinsing on difficult evenings
Wait until permanent teeth arrive to correct technique
Let the child practise, then provide adult brushing assistance
why: Independence before adequate dexterity can leave plaque behind.
Rinsing does not replace cleaning tooth surfaces.
Primary teeth also need effective plaque removal.
Shared participation supports skill-building while ensuring cleaning.
takeaway: Combine child participation with adult help until brushing is effective.
learningObjective: Combine child participation with adult help until brushing is effective.

title: Toddler feeding autonomy
stem: Which approaches support a healthy toddler's feeding autonomy? Select all that apply.
options: Offer regular meals and snacks
Provide appropriate nutritious choices
Let appetite guide how much is eaten from offered food
Require a clean plate before leaving every meal
why: Predictable opportunities support appetite and feeding routines.
Adults can structure available choices without coercion.
Respecting appetite supports developing internal intake regulation.
Clean-plate pressure overrides fullness and can create conflict.
takeaway: Provide mealtime structure while respecting the toddler's appetite.
learningObjective: Provide mealtime structure while respecting the toddler's appetite.

title: Toilet learning readiness
stem: A caregiver wants to begin toilet learning, but the toddler cannot signal needs and strongly resists sitting. What is the best advice?
options: Extend toilet sitting until the child urinates
Pause pressure and watch for readiness while using a predictable routine
Remove fluids after lunch to reduce accidents
Start nighttime training before daytime learning
why: Prolonged forced sitting can increase resistance.
Readiness-based practice supports cooperation and avoids unnecessary conflict.
Fluid restriction does not teach toileting skills.
Nighttime control develops differently and is not a prerequisite.
takeaway: Match toilet learning to developmental readiness.
learningObjective: Match toilet learning to developmental readiness.

title: Toddler choice-making
stem: A two-year-old resists dressing before a clinic visit. Which suggestion best supports autonomy within a necessary routine?
options: Ask whether the child wants to get dressed
Explain every future consequence in detail
Offer a choice between two suitable shirts
Let the child decide whether to attend the visit
why: An unrestricted yes-or-no choice can conflict with the required task.
Lengthy explanations exceed typical toddler processing needs.
Limited acceptable choices support autonomy without abandoning the routine.
Attendance decisions remain an adult responsibility.
takeaway: Offer bounded choices during toddler care routines.
learningObjective: Offer bounded choices during toddler care routines.

title: Preschool procedure preparation
stem: A four-year-old needs a routine blood draw later today. Which preparation is most appropriate?
options: Demonstrate the steps on a doll shortly beforehand
Use a detailed circulation diagram to explain the tests
Give the parent a preparation booklet to read with the child
Show a detailed video of an adult blood collection
why: Brief concrete demonstration can include honest simple descriptions of sensations appropriate to a preschooler.
Detailed internal anatomy may exceed this child's immediate developmental need.
A booklet can supplement teaching, but observed play allows the nurse to gauge this child's understanding before today's procedure.
An adult-focused detailed video may provide less developmentally suitable preparation.
takeaway: Prepare preschoolers with brief concrete play-based explanations.
learningObjective: Prepare preschoolers with brief concrete play-based explanations.

title: Magical thinking about illness
stem: A preschooler says, 'My brother got sick because I was angry at him.' What should the nurse explain?
options: Explain that angry feelings are normal, then change the subject
Explain the disease mechanism using detailed medical terms
Invite the child to help the brother as a way to make amends
Feelings and thoughts did not cause the brother's illness
why: Emotional reassurance alone does not correct the belief that thoughts caused illness.
Technical detail may not address the preschooler's concrete misconception.
Making amends implies that the child caused harm and reinforces guilt.
A concrete correction addresses preschool magical thinking and guilt.
takeaway: Correct preschool beliefs that thoughts or feelings caused illness.
learningObjective: Correct preschool beliefs that thoughts or feelings caused illness.

title: Supporting a school-age learner
stem: Which teaching approaches fit a school-age child learning routine asthma self-care with caregivers? Select all that apply.
options: Explain cause and effect in concrete terms
Allow supervised skill practice
Agree on manageable responsibilities
Give the child sole responsibility for obtaining refills
why: Concrete explanations connect actions with understandable outcomes.
Practice builds confidence and reveals learning needs.
Shared manageable tasks support developing competence.
Adults remain responsible for ensuring access and appropriate oversight.
takeaway: Build school-age self-care through explanation, practice and shared responsibility.
learningObjective: Build school-age self-care through explanation, practice and shared responsibility.

title: School avoidance assessment
stem: A ten-year-old has recurrent morning abdominal discomfort and missed school; initial medical assessment is reassuring. What should the nurse do next?
options: Review the breakfast and symptom diary
Ask the child about school and peer experiences
Begin a school-attendance reward plan
Ask the parent about school experiences
why: Dietary review is relevant but the school-linked pattern also needs the child's account of school and peer experiences.
Contextual assessment may identify stress, bullying or unmet learning needs.
Behavioural incentives may miss bullying, learning difficulties or other reasons for distress.
The parent's account is useful, but the child may know concerns that have not been disclosed at home.
takeaway: Explore school and social context when symptoms interfere with attendance.
learningObjective: Explore school and social context when symptoms interfere with attendance.

title: Screen habits in early childhood
stem: A preschooler watches videos during most meals and bedtime routines. Parents want one useful starting change. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Replace all videos with educational content only
Allow screens whenever the child is quiet
Create screen-free meals and a calming bedtime routine
Move the device to the living room while keeping the same viewing schedule
why: Content choice does not address displacement of interaction and sleep routines.
Quiet behaviour alone does not establish a healthy pattern.
Specific routine changes protect interaction and sleep-related habits.
Changing location does not address displacement of meals and bedtime routines.
takeaway: Focus screen counselling on routines and activities displaced by use.
learningObjective: Focus screen counselling on routines and activities displaced by use.

title: Childhood activity access
stem: A parent cannot afford organized sports and worries their child cannot be active. Which advice is best?
options: Plan enjoyable free play, walking or community activities
Delay activity until a sports program is affordable
Prioritize exercise equipment purchases over daily play
Use competitive performance as the first activity goal
why: Everyday enjoyable movement can support activity without program fees.
Waiting leaves an unnecessary access barrier in place.
Equipment is not required for many beneficial activities.
Performance goals may reduce enjoyment and participation.
takeaway: Develop feasible enjoyable movement opportunities beyond organized sports.
learningObjective: Develop feasible enjoyable movement opportunities beyond organized sports.

title: A childhood growth conversation
stem: A child is distressed after being called overweight at school. The caregiver requests a diet plan. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Set a rapid weight-loss goal before assessing growth
Ask the child to weigh daily without support
Discuss appearance as the main reason for change
Assess growth and routines using nonstigmatizing family-centred language
why: Rapid restriction without assessment may be inappropriate during growth.
Frequent unsupervised weighing may intensify distress.
Appearance-focused counselling reinforces the child's experience of stigma.
Growth context and respectful family routines support a safer plan.
takeaway: Discuss childhood growth without stigma or unassessed restrictive dieting.
learningObjective: Discuss childhood growth without stigma or unassessed restrictive dieting.

title: Preparing for puberty
stem: Which topics belong in anticipatory guidance before or during early puberty? Select all that apply.
options: Expected variation in timing of body changes
Private questions about hygiene and menstruation where relevant
Trusted adults and reliable information sources
Comparison with classmates to determine whether development is acceptable
why: Normal variation can reduce unnecessary anxiety about peer differences.
Private practical information supports preparation for body changes.
Accessible trusted support helps the young person seek help.
Peer comparison alone cannot evaluate development or respect privacy.
takeaway: Offer private practical puberty guidance that acknowledges normal variation.
learningObjective: Offer private practical puberty guidance that acknowledges normal variation.

title: Adolescent consultation privacy
stem: A teenager becomes silent when a parent answers sexual-health questions. What is the best initial approach in a routine visit?
options: Continue with the parent to avoid discomfort
Explain the routine opportunity for private discussion and confidentiality limits
Have the teenager and parent complete the sensitive-topic questionnaire together
Offer a take-home sexual-health questionnaire
why: Continuing without privacy may prevent accurate assessment.
A normalized private discussion supports disclosure while clarifying limits.
A shared questionnaire does not provide a confidential opportunity to speak.
A routine private conversation offers timely supported disclosure and clarification of confidentiality.
takeaway: Provide developmentally appropriate privacy with clear confidentiality limits.
learningObjective: Provide developmentally appropriate privacy with clear confidentiality limits.

title: Sexual-health assessment language
stem: A young adult says they have partners of more than one gender. Which question best guides relevant prevention teaching?
options: 'Which identity should I use to decide your risk?'
'Can we skip details if you have no symptoms?'
'What sexual practices and protection methods are relevant for you?'
'Does one partner seem safer than the others?'
why: Identity alone does not describe exposures or protection.
Absence of symptoms does not rule out infection risk.
Practice-based questions allow individualized and inclusive prevention advice.
Perceived safety is not a substitute for exposure assessment.
takeaway: Base sexual-health counselling on practices and protection rather than identity assumptions.
learningObjective: Base sexual-health counselling on practices and protection rather than identity assumptions.

title: STI screening without symptoms
stem: A client with a new partner says no testing is needed because both feel well. What should the nurse explain?
options: Some infections are asymptomatic, so testing depends on exposure and current guidance
Testing is useful only when a rash is present
A partner's reassurance replaces screening
Screening is required only when contraception fails
why: Risk-based screening may identify infections without noticeable symptoms.
Symptoms are not required for an infection to be present.
Reassurance cannot establish infection status.
Pregnancy prevention and infection screening address different concerns.
takeaway: Explain why asymptomatic clients may still benefit from STI screening.
learningObjective: Explain why asymptomatic clients may still benefit from STI screening.

title: Contraception and infection prevention
stem: A client using an intrauterine contraceptive begins a new relationship. What should teaching emphasize?
options: The device protects against common sexually transmitted infections
Screening can replace all barrier use
Reassure the client if the new partner has no symptoms
Pregnancy prevention and infection prevention may require different strategies
why: An intrauterine contraceptive does not provide barrier protection from infection.
Testing does not prevent future exposure.
Asymptomatic infection is possible, so symptom absence does not replace prevention and screening advice.
A separate discussion of condoms and testing addresses the new exposure context.
takeaway: Distinguish contraceptive effectiveness from protection against infection.
learningObjective: Distinguish contraceptive effectiveness from protection against infection.

title: Adolescent self-management transition
stem: Which actions support a teenager preparing to manage a chronic condition more independently? Select all that apply.
options: Practise describing the condition in their own words
Rehearse booking appointments with support
Develop a medication and refill plan
Transfer every task immediately because adult transfer is approaching
why: Clear explanation supports participation in future care.
Supported practice builds navigation skills before full independence.
Planning anticipates a common source of treatment interruption.
Abrupt transfer may exceed current skills and support.
takeaway: Build health-management independence gradually before transfer to adult care.
learningObjective: Build health-management independence gradually before transfer to adult care.

title: Menstrual symptom assessment
stem: A teenager reports missing school because of heavy menstrual bleeding and fatigue. What is the best nursing response?
options: Normalize all menstrual variation without assessment
Arrange clinical assessment of bleeding and possible anemia
Recommend waiting until cycles have continued for several years
Focus only on school attendance expectations
why: Functional impairment and fatigue warrant more than reassurance.
The pattern suggests a need to assess severity and consequences.
Delay may prolong treatable symptoms or anemia.
Attendance counselling alone does not address the health concern.
takeaway: Assess heavy menstrual bleeding that impairs function or causes fatigue.
learningObjective: Assess heavy menstrual bleeding that impairs function or causes fatigue.

title: Exercise and menstrual change
stem: An adolescent runner has increased training, restricted intake and stopped menstruating. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Recommend a daily calcium supplement
Reassure that absent periods confirm athletic fitness
Arrange assessment of energy availability and overall health
Refer for discussion of hormonal cycle regulation
why: A single nutrient intervention can miss broader low energy availability and other causes of amenorrhea.
Menstrual cessation is not a reliable marker of healthy fitness.
Training, restriction and amenorrhea warrant nutritional and medical review.
Induced bleeding would not identify the cause or address the broader health concern.
takeaway: Recognize menstrual change with restricted intake as a health concern in athletes.
learningObjective: Recognize menstrual change with restricted intake as a health concern in athletes.

title: Vaping misconception
stem: A student who has never smoked uses nicotine vapes to manage exam stress. Which response best supports health promotion?
options: Explore dependence and stress triggers while offering cessation support
Recommend continuing because smoking would be worse
Focus only on flavour preference
Advise switching brands before assessing use
why: Assessment can address nicotine exposure and the coping function of use.
Comparison with smoking does not make nicotine initiation beneficial.
Flavour alone does not characterize dependence or coping needs.
Brand changes do not address continued nicotine use.
takeaway: Address nicotine use and the stress-related reasons for it together.
learningObjective: Address nicotine use and the stress-related reasons for it together.

title: Tanning and skin health
stem: A young adult uses tanning beds before vacation to obtain a protective base tan. What should the nurse explain?
options: A base tan removes the need for sunscreen
Indoor tanning can safely prepare skin if sessions are brief
Skin protection matters only after redness develops
Tanning adds ultraviolet exposure; plan shade, clothing and sunscreen instead
why: Tanning does not provide reliable protection from further ultraviolet injury.
Brief sessions still add ultraviolet exposure.
Skin injury can occur before visible redness.
Multiple protective strategies reduce exposure without deliberate tanning.
takeaway: Replace deliberate tanning with practical ultraviolet protection.
learningObjective: Replace deliberate tanning with practical ultraviolet protection.

title: Youth sleep routine
stem: Which changes may help a teenager whose late-night phone use is reducing sleep? Select all that apply.
options: Establish a consistent wake time
Move stimulating screen use away from bedtime
Create a wind-down routine
Use energy drinks to replace lost sleep on weekdays
why: A regular wake time supports a stable sleep schedule.
Reducing bedtime stimulation supports settling for sleep.
Predictable quiet activity can signal the transition to sleep.
Stimulants do not replace sleep and can perpetuate sleep difficulty.
takeaway: Develop consistent routines that protect adequate adolescent sleep.
learningObjective: Develop consistent routines that protect adequate adolescent sleep.

title: Interpreting screening results
stem: An asymptomatic client receives an abnormal screening result and asks whether cancer is certain. What should the nurse explain?
options: Screening alone establishes the final diagnosis
Further diagnostic assessment is needed to clarify the result
A lack of symptoms proves the result is false
Repeating the same screening at home replaces follow-up
why: Screening identifies people needing further evaluation rather than confirming every diagnosis.
Diagnostic follow-up determines what an abnormal result means.
Some conditions are detectable before symptoms develop.
The recommended follow-up cannot automatically be replaced by repeat screening.
takeaway: Distinguish an abnormal screening result from a confirmed diagnosis.
learningObjective: Distinguish an abnormal screening result from a confirmed diagnosis.

title: Symptoms despite recent screening
stem: A client with recent normal colorectal screening now reports persistent rectal bleeding. What advice is best?
options: Wait until the next routine screening interval
Repeat the same screening without clinical review
Seek assessment of the new symptom
Assume hemorrhoids because screening was normal
why: Routine intervals apply to screening, not evaluation of new symptoms.
Symptom assessment may require a different diagnostic pathway.
New persistent bleeding warrants assessment despite a prior normal screen.
A normal screening result does not establish the cause of bleeding.
takeaway: Evaluate new symptoms independently of routine screening schedules.
learningObjective: Evaluate new symptoms independently of routine screening schedules.

title: Family history and screening
stem: A client reports several close relatives with early-onset cancer but has not reached the routine population screening age. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange individualized risk review rather than applying age criteria alone
Reassure that age rules exclude all screening needs
Recommend every available tumour-marker blood test
Base advice only on the oldest affected relative
why: A significant family pattern can change risk assessment and planning.
Average-risk age criteria may not fit this family history.
Broad unselected testing is not a substitute for risk-based assessment.
Multiple relatives and ages contribute to the pattern.
takeaway: Identify family histories that require individualized screening advice.
learningObjective: Identify family histories that require individualized screening advice.

title: Informed screening choice
stem: A capable client is uncertain about an offered screening test. What should the nurse discuss?
options: Only the benefits to improve acceptance
Only the worst possible outcome of declining
The nurse's personal screening decisions
Potential benefits, harms, follow-up and the client's preferences
why: Benefits alone do not support a balanced informed choice.
Fear-based framing can distort rather than inform the decision.
The nurse's choices do not determine the client's values.
Balanced information and preferences support shared decision-making.
takeaway: Support informed screening choices with benefits, harms and follow-up information.
learningObjective: Support informed screening choices with benefits, harms and follow-up information.

title: Findings before an injected vaccine
stem: Before an indicated injected non-live vaccine, which findings require additional clarification or assessment before proceeding? Select all that apply.
options: Previous anaphylaxis after the same vaccine product
Mild afebrile runny nose in an otherwise well client
Current significant febrile illness
Brief soreness after a previous injection
Antibiotic use alone without a relevant active illness
why: A severe prior reaction requires product-specific safety assessment.
Minor illness alone generally does not require deferral.
Significant acute illness warrants evaluation of vaccine timing and the illness itself.
Brief local soreness is not equivalent to a severe allergic reaction.
Antibiotic use alone does not usually preclude an injected non-live vaccine.
takeaway: Distinguish findings requiring vaccine review from common noncontraindications.
learningObjective: Distinguish findings requiring vaccine review from common noncontraindications.

title: A minor illness before vaccination
stem: A well-appearing child has a mild runny nose without fever and is due for routine vaccines. What should the nurse do?
options: Cancel automatically until all nasal symptoms disappear
Assess against vaccine-specific guidance rather than assuming a contraindication
Begin antibiotics before vaccination
Require a negative respiratory panel for every vaccine
why: Mild illness alone is not generally a reason to defer routine immunization.
Clinical assessment and current guidance determine whether vaccination can proceed.
Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for this presentation.
Routine testing is not generally required solely for vaccination.
takeaway: Distinguish minor illness from vaccine-specific precautions requiring deferral.
learningObjective: Distinguish minor illness from vaccine-specific precautions requiring deferral.

title: Vaccine record gaps
stem: A newcomer has incomplete vaccine documentation and is unsure which doses were given. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Assume childhood infection provides complete protection
Restart every vaccine without checking recommendations
Review available records and arrange an individualized catch-up assessment
Defer discussion until records can be obtained from every previous residence
why: Infection history does not establish protection against all vaccine-preventable diseases.
Catch-up decisions should follow vaccine-specific guidance and verified information.
Review allows an appropriate plan despite uncertainty.
Indefinite delay may leave preventable protection gaps.
takeaway: Use current catch-up guidance when immunization records are incomplete.
learningObjective: Use current catch-up guidance when immunization records are incomplete.

title: Vaccine reaction interpretation
stem: After a previous vaccine, an adult had a sore arm for a day without systemic symptoms. They now believe all vaccines are contraindicated. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the reaction and explain expected local effects
Arrange an automatic vaccine-allergy referral
Recommend changing vaccine brands for future doses
Recommend antihistamine premedication for future doses
why: Brief local soreness supports counselling about expected effects after confirming the absence of severe features.
This isolated local symptom does not itself establish a need for specialist allergy referral.
A brand change is not indicated solely by ordinary brief local soreness.
Premedication does not address the misconception that expected soreness is a severe allergy.
takeaway: Clarify prior reactions before labelling a vaccine contraindication.
learningObjective: Clarify prior reactions before labelling a vaccine contraindication.

title: Travel preparation timing
stem: An adult with a chronic condition is planning international travel in two months. What is the most useful health-promotion advice?
options: Obtain vaccine advice during the departure-week refill
Prepare an extra supply of regular medicines
Print the destination health advisory
Book an individualized travel-health appointment now
why: Departure-week advice may leave insufficient time for some preventive measures.
Medication supply matters but does not cover itinerary-specific risks and preventive planning.
A general advisory does not integrate this client's condition and exact itinerary.
Early review allows time to coordinate prevention and practical management for the chronic condition.
takeaway: Arrange travel-health preparation early enough for individualized preventive measures.
learningObjective: Arrange travel-health preparation early enough for individualized preventive measures.

title: Adult vaccine review
stem: Which factors help determine an adult's immunization needs? Select all that apply.
options: Age and previous doses
Health conditions and treatment
Occupational or travel exposures
Whether childhood records contain at least one vaccine
why: Age and dose history shape routine and catch-up recommendations.
Some conditions change risk, timing or product suitability.
Specific exposures may create additional indications.
One recorded dose does not establish complete current protection.
takeaway: Review adult vaccination using history, health status and exposure risks.
learningObjective: Review adult vaccination using history, health status and exposure risks.

title: Selecting the teaching priority
stem: Before discharge, a client correctly demonstrates wound cleansing, dressing placement and moisture protection and has supplies. They cannot identify concerning changes. What teaching has highest priority?
options: Reconfirm where replacement dressings can be purchased
Review changes requiring help and the contact route
Repeat the demonstrated dressing sequence
Rehearse shower-cover placement once more
why: Supply access is already established and is not the demonstrated gap.
Recognition and access teaching addresses the remaining safety need.
The routine sequence has already been demonstrated correctly.
Moisture protection is established; escalation knowledge remains missing.
takeaway: Prioritize the demonstrated safety gap after routine skills are established.
learningObjective: Prioritize the demonstrated safety gap after routine skills are established.

title: Assessing practical learning barriers
stem: A client correctly describes medication timing, has supplies, opens packaging easily and reports no adverse effects. Morning doses are missed while helping a spouse dress. What should the nurse explore first?
options: Whether prescription costs are creating a barrier
Whether medication effects discourage morning use
How dosing fits the caregiving routine
Whether a different container would be easier to open
why: Current supply is available and cost is not the stated obstacle.
No adverse effects are reported; the timing conflict is explicit.
The missed doses coincide with competing caregiving tasks.
Packaging is manageable and does not explain this pattern.
takeaway: Target the practical barrier supported by the client's account.
learningObjective: Target the practical barrier supported by the client's account.

title: Independent monitoring with arthritis
stem: A client understands glucose monitoring but cannot open the current strip package because of arthritis. They want independence and have no helper at testing times. What is the best next plan?
options: Assess accessible packaging or a suitable alternative device
Ask a relative to prepare every test at dosing time
Repeat practice opening the same package for another week
Arrange all monitoring through scheduled home visits
why: An equipment adaptation directly addresses the barrier while preserving the stated goal.
No helper is available at the required times.
Repetition alone may not overcome the mechanical limitation.
Full service takeover may be unnecessary if a feasible adaptation exists.
takeaway: Assess equipment adaptations before replacing feasible independent self-care.
learningObjective: Assess equipment adaptations before replacing feasible independent self-care.

title: Evaluating a practical skill
stem: After catheter-care teaching, a client describes every step correctly but contaminates the equipment during practice. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The teaching objective is met because recall is accurate
Another pamphlet is sufficient evidence of correction
Performance can be assumed to improve at home
Practical competence requires further coached practice and reassessment
why: Accurate recall does not establish safe task performance.
Receiving information is not evidence of corrected technique.
Unobserved future improvement cannot be assumed.
The observed error identifies a specific skill needing practice.
takeaway: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.
learningObjective: Evaluate demonstrated performance separately from verbal knowledge.

title: Interpreter-supported teaching
stem: A client prefers a language the nurse does not speak. Which approaches support accurate teaching with a qualified interpreter? Select all that apply.
options: Speak directly to the client
Pause after short segments
Ask the interpreter to decide which care instructions matter
Use a family member to verify confidential answers without asking the client
why: Direct engagement preserves the therapeutic relationship.
Short segments support accurate interpretation and questions.
Clinical priorities remain the responsibility of the care team and client.
Involving relatives requires attention to client preference and privacy.
takeaway: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.
learningObjective: Use qualified interpretation while communicating directly with the client.

title: A decimal misunderstanding in measurement
stem: A caregiver reads a prescribed 0.5 mL dose aloud as 5 mL before using the supplied oral syringe. What should the nurse do first?
options: Clarify the dose reading and guide a correct measurement demonstration
Request a new medication concentration immediately
Replace the syringe with a measuring cup
Repeat the medicine's purpose before another demonstration
why: The tenfold verbal error requires correcting decimal interpretation and then checking practical measurement.
A concentration change may not resolve the demonstrated interpretation problem.
A cup is less suitable for a small volume and does not correct the misunderstanding.
The medicine's purpose does not explain the incorrect dose reading.
takeaway: Clarify the meaning of the prescribed volume when demonstration reveals a decimal error.
learningObjective: Clarify the meaning of the prescribed volume when demonstration reveals a decimal error.

title: Organizing complex instructions
stem: A client receiving instructions from three services says the separate leaflets conflict and they cannot identify the first home-care task. What is most useful?
options: Review all leaflets verbally in one uninterrupted session
Provide the complete technical discharge summary
Create a coordinated prioritized action checklist and practise its first steps
Give a separate booklet from each additional specialist
why: An uninterrupted review may preserve the fragmentation and overload.
A technical summary may not translate recommendations into usable actions.
Coordination resolves sequence and consistency before practice checks usability.
More disconnected information may worsen the stated problem.
takeaway: Coordinate competing instructions into a usable prioritized action plan.
learningObjective: Coordinate competing instructions into a usable prioritized action plan.

title: Teaching after a sensory change
stem: A client newly using reading glasses is learning ostomy care and avoids the printed guide. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Whether the client can see the material and equipment comfortably
Whether the client agrees with every instruction
Whether family help is available for reading the guide
What the client already knows about ostomy care
why: Visual access may explain avoidance and can often be improved.
Agreement does not establish access to the teaching materials.
Family support may help, but the new visual barrier should first be assessed directly.
Prior knowledge matters, but new glasses and avoided print specifically suggest an access issue.
takeaway: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.
learningObjective: Assess sensory access before interpreting limited engagement as resistance.

title: A missed learning goal
stem: A client agreed to practise a dressing change but cannot complete it after teaching. What is the best nursing response?
options: Record the goal as achieved because teaching occurred
Label the client unwilling before reassessment
Repeat the identical session without examining the difficulty
Identify the difficult steps and adapt the teaching plan
why: Teaching delivery is not equivalent to learning achievement.
Difficulty may reflect a skill, access or readiness problem.
Unchanged repetition may leave the actual barrier untouched.
Step-specific assessment supports targeted coaching and reevaluation.
takeaway: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.
learningObjective: Revise teaching from observed learning difficulties.

title: Health app appraisal
stem: A client wants an app to record migraine patterns for appointments. Which findings support choosing an app for this purpose? Select all that apply.
options: It exports the symptom records needed for appointments
Its advice identifies credible sources
A high user rating establishes medical accuracy
Its privacy terms explain data use and are acceptable to the client
Popularity confirms the intended clinical function
why: Relevant usable records support the stated appointment goal.
Identifiable evidence helps assess accompanying clinical advice.
User ratings do not independently establish medical accuracy.
Understandable acceptable terms support an informed privacy choice, although they do not guarantee security.
Popularity does not establish suitability for the intended task.
takeaway: Evaluate a health app's purpose, evidence and privacy.
learningObjective: Evaluate a health app's purpose, evidence and privacy.

title: Setting an initial walking goal
stem: An inactive adult comfortably walks five minutes and wants to build a routine. Which initial plan best supports achievable progress over the next two weeks?
options: Resume the 30-minute daily route used several years ago
Agree on short scheduled walks and review tolerance after two weeks
Walk whenever motivation is high and record only the longest outing
Add distance every day to meet a preset target by day fourteen
why: A past capacity may exceed the current baseline.
The plan is specific, feasible and allows adjustment from actual response.
Irregular motivation-based activity may not build the desired routine.
Automatic increases may outpace tolerance and undermine persistence.
takeaway: Start activity goals from current capacity with planned review.
learningObjective: Start activity goals from current capacity with planned review.

title: Exploring ambivalence
stem: A client says, 'I know smoking harms me, but it helps me get through work.' What response best supports motivation?
options: List complications until the client agrees to quit
Set a quit date without discussion
Ask what the client likes and dislikes about smoking
Focus on whether coworkers approve of smoking
why: More warnings may not address the competing value the client describes.
An imposed goal may not reflect readiness.
Exploring both sides helps the client articulate reasons for change.
Coworker approval is less relevant than the client's goals and barriers.
takeaway: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.
learningObjective: Explore ambivalence before prescribing a behaviour-change goal.

title: Learning from a smoking lapse
stem: After two weeks without smoking, a client smoked during an argument and feels the attempt is ruined. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: Review the trigger and adjust the quit plan
Restart the same quit plan
Reassess whether the client is ready to quit
Review the number of cigarettes smoked since the argument
why: A lapse can identify coping supports needed for the next attempt.
Restarting alone may miss the coping gap revealed by the argument.
Readiness can be explored, but a single lapse does not establish loss of motivation; the identified trigger provides a concrete place to revise the current effort.
Quantity alone does not explain the trigger or recovery plan.
takeaway: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.
learningObjective: Use a lapse to refine cessation strategies rather than abandon the goal.

title: Changing sugary drink intake
stem: A client chooses replacing one daily soft drink with water as a first goal. What is the best nursing response?
options: Add several food changes to the goal at the same visit
Use daily weight as the main measure of the substitution
Provide general dietary education before specifying the routine
Confirm when the substitution will occur and how progress will be reviewed
why: Additional simultaneous goals may reduce feasibility before the chosen habit is established.
Weight change does not directly show whether the planned drink substitution occurred.
Information alone does not identify the cue and action needed for this chosen change.
A concrete cue and review plan strengthen implementation.
takeaway: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.
learningObjective: Turn a chosen health behaviour into a practical routine and review plan.

title: Supporting tobacco cessation
stem: Which assessments help tailor a client's quit plan? Select all that apply.
options: Times and situations associated with smoking
Previous strategies that helped or failed
Whether the client meets the nurse's preferred quit date
Only the brand and purchase location
why: Trigger patterns identify where coping strategies are needed.
Past experience can reveal effective supports and barriers.
Goals should reflect collaborative planning rather than the nurse's preference.
Product details alone do not capture dependence or readiness.
takeaway: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.
learningObjective: Tailor cessation support using triggers and prior attempts.

title: Adapting activity with knee pain
stem: A client with stable osteoarthritis develops knee pain during long walks but tolerates gentle cycling. They want better endurance. Which plan fits best?
options: Repeat the long walk daily until endurance improves
Agree on a lower-impact cycling trial with appropriate guidance
Use stretching alone as the endurance program
Pause activity until every episode of knee discomfort has ended
why: Repeating the painful load may reduce participation without addressing tolerability.
A tolerated lower-impact option can support the endurance goal.
Stretching alone does not provide equivalent endurance training.
Complete delay may worsen conditioning when a tolerable option exists.
takeaway: Match activity type to tolerated loading and the client's functional goal.
learningObjective: Match activity type to tolerated loading and the client's functional goal.

title: Activity after deconditioning
stem: After prolonged illness, a client walks only to the end of the corridor before tiring but wants to resume an old 40-minute route. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Resume the old route using the previous pace
Return on the date originally planned before the illness
Build gradually from current tolerance with the recovery team
Use flexibility exercises alone as the endurance plan
why: The old workload exceeds the stated current capacity.
Calendar timing does not establish regained function.
Graded progression reflects present ability and the endurance goal.
Flexibility may help movement but does not fully address endurance.
takeaway: Base post-illness activity progression on present function.
learningObjective: Base post-illness activity progression on present function.

title: Prolonged sitting at work
stem: A desk worker exercises on weekends but sits uninterrupted for several hours each workday. Which change most directly addresses the remaining pattern?
options: Schedule brief movement breaks during the workday
Add a longer exercise session on Saturday
Stand continuously at the same workstation all day
Record total weekly steps
why: Regular movement interrupts the prolonged sedentary periods identified.
Weekend exercise does not directly interrupt workday sitting.
Prolonged static standing is not the same as varied movement.
Tracking alone does not change uninterrupted sitting.
takeaway: Address long sedentary periods alongside planned exercise.
learningObjective: Address long sedentary periods alongside planned exercise.

title: Improving plant-food iron absorption
stem: A vegetarian client is improving dietary iron intake and often eats lentils at lunch. Which addition best supports absorption of the iron in that meal?
options: Tea served with the meal
A calcium supplement taken with the meal
Coffee immediately after the meal
Sweet peppers or another vitamin-C-rich food
why: Tea can reduce absorption of nonheme iron when taken with the meal.
Calcium taken with iron-rich meals may reduce iron absorption.
Coffee can inhibit nonheme iron absorption around the meal.
Vitamin C enhances absorption of iron from plant foods.
takeaway: Pair plant iron sources with vitamin-C-rich foods.
learningObjective: Pair plant iron sources with vitamin-C-rich foods.

title: Planning nutritious meals on a budget
stem: Which suggestions may help a client with limited income obtain balanced meals? Select all that apply.
options: Consider affordable frozen or canned foods with suitable labels
Plan meals using available low-cost protein foods
Recommend only fresh specialty produce
Assume all packaged foods have the same nutritional value
why: Appropriate frozen and canned options can be nutritious and affordable.
Feasible protein sources support nutrition within the budget.
Specialty-only advice may be financially inaccessible.
Labels and preparation vary, so blanket assumptions are inaccurate.
takeaway: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.
learningObjective: Adapt nutrition teaching to cost and available food options.

title: Hydration in heat with restrictions
stem: An older adult with a prescribed fluid limit asks how to manage a heat wave. What is the best response?
options: Ignore the limit throughout the heat wave
Seek an individualized fluid and cooling plan from the treating team
Maintain the limit without considering new symptoms
Use sports drinks as unrestricted extra fluid
why: Unsupervised excess intake may worsen the condition requiring restriction.
The plan must balance heat risk with the client's clinical limitations.
Heat may change needs and symptoms requiring reassessment.
Sports drinks still contribute fluid and may add unwanted electrolytes.
takeaway: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.
learningObjective: Individualize heat advice when medical fluid restrictions apply.

title: Protecting sleep during shift work
stem: A night-shift worker's daytime sleep is repeatedly interrupted by household noise and errands. Which plan best addresses the identified cause?
options: Extend sleep on days off while keeping workday arrangements
Wear an eye mask but remain available for daytime errands
Agree on a protected dark quiet sleep period with the household
Replace the main sleep period with brief naps in the living room
why: Catch-up sleep does not remove the recurring workday interruptions.
An eye mask does not address noise or expected availability.
Household agreement and an appropriate environment protect the actual sleep opportunity.
Fragmented naps in a busy setting may not provide adequate consolidated rest.
takeaway: Protect sleep opportunity and environment within shift-work constraints.
learningObjective: Protect sleep opportunity and environment within shift-work constraints.

title: Persistent snoring and sleepiness
stem: A client reports loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses and daytime sleepiness despite enough time in bed. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Clinical assessment for a sleep-related breathing disorder
A larger pillow as the only intervention
More time in bed before mentioning breathing pauses
Caffeine at each meal to improve alertness
why: The combined symptoms warrant evaluation beyond sleep-hygiene advice.
