stem: A client recovering from a stroke reports hopelessness and stops rehabilitation. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume rehabilitation refusal is a fixed preference
Discuss only muscle strength goals
Delay mood assessment until physical recovery is complete
Assess depressive symptoms and barriers while preserving achievable rehabilitation goals
why: Withdrawal may reflect treatable mood or practical difficulties.
Physical goals alone may miss the reason for disengagement.
Mood difficulties can interfere with recovery and deserve timely assessment.
Integrated assessment addresses participation and emotional needs together.
takeaway: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.
learningObjective: Assess mood when hopelessness interferes with physical rehabilitation.

title: Monitoring change during treatment
stem: Which changes during depression treatment require prompt reassessment? Select all that apply.
options: New agitation with suicidal thoughts
Markedly reduced need for sleep with unusual impulsivity
A gradual return to a valued routine
New inability to meet basic intake needs
why: Agitation with suicidality can increase immediate risk.
A possible mood switch needs timely clinical review.
Gradual functional improvement is an expected positive outcome.
Inadequate intake can create urgent physical consequences.
takeaway: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.
learningObjective: Reassess new risk, activation or physical compromise during mood treatment.

title: Sudden calm after suicidal distress
stem: A client recently expressed intense suicidal thoughts and now appears unexpectedly calm after giving away possessions. What should the nurse do?
options: Reduce observation because the mood appears better
Reassess suicide risk promptly and maintain current precautions pending review
Focus only on the donated items' value
Wait for the client to volunteer a new concern
why: Apparent calm does not establish safety and can accompany a decision to act.
The behavioural change requires direct reassessment before reducing protection.
Monetary value is less relevant than the meaning of giving belongings away.
Risk assessment should respond actively to concerning changes.
takeaway: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.
learningObjective: Reassess suicide risk when behaviour changes despite apparent mood improvement.

title: A negative answer with concerning collateral
stem: A client denies suicidal thoughts, but a family member reports recent farewell messages. What is the best response?
options: Disregard the family because the client denied risk
Accept the messages as proof of a specific plan without assessment
Explore the discrepancy and assess risk using all available information
Ask the family to decide discharge readiness
why: Denial alone does not resolve credible concerning information.
Collateral information requires assessment rather than unsupported conclusions.
Combining sources supports a fuller safety evaluation.
Discharge judgment requires the clinical team and applicable processes.
takeaway: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.
learningObjective: Integrate collateral information into suicide-risk assessment.

title: Limits of a safety promise
stem: A client at suicide risk promises, 'I will not hurt myself.' What should the nurse conclude?
options: The promise does not replace assessment, observation or a safety plan
Observation can end immediately
A written version guarantees safety
Further questions would invalidate the promise
why: A promise cannot reliably establish risk level or substitute for protection.
Precaution changes require reassessment and appropriate clinical decisions.
Signing does not transform a promise into a guarantee.
Direct ongoing assessment remains necessary and supportive.
takeaway: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Do not use a no-harm promise as a substitute for suicide assessment.

title: Meaningful protective factors
stem: A client says caring for a pet helps them resist suicidal thoughts but also reports an active plan. What should the nurse recognize?
options: A protective relationship eliminates current risk
Only the plan matters and the pet is irrelevant
Discussing the pet replaces assessment of intent
The protective factor is useful but does not cancel the active risk
why: Protective factors do not guarantee safety when acute risks remain.
Protective connections may contribute to a future safety plan.
Intent and access still require direct assessment.
Both risk and protective information belong in the clinical formulation.
takeaway: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.
learningObjective: Assess protective factors without treating them as guarantees against suicide.

title: Elements of a safety plan
stem: Which components belong in a collaborative suicide safety plan? Select all that apply.
options: Personal warning signs and coping actions
People and services the client can contact
A promise that no crisis will recur
Steps to reduce access to means of self-harm
why: Recognizable cues and coping steps support early action.
Practical contacts provide escalating sources of help.
Recurrence cannot be ruled out by agreement.
Reducing access is an important preventive component.
takeaway: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.
learningObjective: Build a practical safety plan with warning signs, coping, contacts and means safety.

title: Practising a crisis plan
stem: A client can name their safety-plan contacts but says they would not know what to say during distress. What should the nurse do?
options: Add more phone numbers without discussion
Rehearse a brief help-seeking message with the client
Remove contacts the client feels nervous about using
Assume written numbers alone are sufficient
why: More numbers do not address the communication barrier.
Rehearsal makes the plan easier to use during crisis.
Nervousness may be addressed rather than automatically eliminating support.
Knowing a number does not establish ability to use it.
takeaway: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.
learningObjective: Practise how to request help as part of safety planning.

title: Confidentiality and acute risk
stem: A client discloses an imminent self-harm plan but asks the nurse to tell nobody. What should the nurse explain?
options: Everything must remain secret if the client requests it
Disclosure will be made to every staff member in the facility
Necessary people must be involved to protect safety, with the client informed as possible
Only a family member can authorize a safety response
why: Confidentiality is not absolute when immediate safety is threatened.
Information should be shared for legitimate safety needs, not indiscriminately.
Transparent limited sharing supports safety and trust.
Emergency safety actions do not depend solely on family authorization.
takeaway: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.
learningObjective: Explain necessary safety-related sharing without promising absolute secrecy.

title: Supervision during an urgent assessment
stem: A client under ordered continuous observation for acute suicide risk needs transfer for assessment. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Maintain the prescribed observation through a clear supervised handoff
Send the client ahead while staff arrange paperwork
Substitute a family visit for observation without review
Reduce supervision because the receiving unit is secure
why: Transitions must preserve the established protective observation level.
Unsupervised gaps undermine the purpose of continuous observation.
Family presence does not automatically replace clinical requirements.
Unit design alone does not authorize a precaution change.
takeaway: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.
learningObjective: Maintain suicide precautions across transitions until appropriately reassessed.

title: Asking about access to means
stem: A client reports intermittent suicidal thoughts without describing a method. Why should the nurse ask about access to potentially harmful items?
options: To determine whether the client is being truthful by surprise
To complete a form without discussing the answer
To decide whether emotional support is unnecessary
To understand risk and plan practical steps to reduce access
why: The purpose is assessment and safety, not catching the client out.
Responses need clinical interpretation and follow-through.
Means assessment complements rather than replaces emotional support.
Available means influence immediate safety planning.
takeaway: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.
learningObjective: Assess access to means to guide concrete protective actions.

title: Evaluating a proposed discharge safety plan
stem: Which findings indicate that a safety plan needs revision before it can be relied upon? Select all that apply.
options: The only listed contact is unreachable overnight
The client cannot access the promised follow-up service
The client identifies a personal early warning sign
A support person agreed to a role without knowing what it involves
why: An unavailable contact creates a predictable access gap.
A plan depending on inaccessible care is not operational.
Recognizing a warning sign supports plan usefulness.
Support roles need clear agreement and practical understanding.
takeaway: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.
learningObjective: Verify that safety-plan resources are reachable and understood.

title: Self-injury without stated suicidal intent
stem: A client reports cutting to relieve distress and denies wanting to die. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess injuries, function of self-injury and suicide risk
Assume suicide risk is absent because intent is denied
Focus only on stopping the behaviour through criticism
Delay wound assessment until counselling is completed
why: Physical care and direct risk assessment are both necessary.
Nonsuicidal intent does not eliminate concurrent or future suicide risk.
Criticism may increase shame and reduce disclosure.
Injuries require timely assessment regardless of behavioural purpose.
takeaway: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.
learningObjective: Assess both physical injury and suicide risk after self-injury.

title: Responding after self-injury disclosure
stem: After wounds are assessed, a client says, 'You must think I am attention-seeking.' What response is most therapeutic?
options: 'You should have used a different method.'
'I want to understand the distress and what helps you stay safe.'
'We should avoid discussing the behaviour again.'
'Your family can decide whether the distress is real.'
why: Method comparison is not a therapeutic response to distress.
Nonjudgmental exploration supports trust and safer coping.
Avoidance prevents assessment of the behaviour's function.
The client's distress does not require family validation.
takeaway: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.
learningObjective: Respond to self-injury with nonjudgmental assessment of distress and safety.

title: Choosing safer coping alternatives
stem: A client who self-injures identifies rising tension before episodes. What should the nurse do within the treatment plan?
options: Recommend suppressing every feeling without support
Select a coping method without asking preferences
Rehearse agreed noninjurious strategies at the early-tension stage
Wait until another injury before discussing coping
why: Suppression alone may not provide effective regulation.
Strategies need to be acceptable and feasible for the client.
Early practice links identifiable cues with safer responses.
Waiting misses an opportunity for prevention.
takeaway: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.
learningObjective: Connect early self-harm cues with rehearsed noninjurious coping.

title: Digital messages suggesting risk
stem: A client shows farewell messages they drafted but did not send and says they feel embarrassed. What is the best response?
options: Explore intent, timing, current thoughts and safety needs directly
Reassure solely because the messages were not sent
Focus on deleting the messages before assessment
Ask whether the writing is grammatically clear
why: Preparatory communication can indicate risk and warrants direct assessment.
Lack of sending does not establish absence of intent.
Deletion does not evaluate or resolve the underlying risk.
Editing details are unrelated to immediate safety needs.
takeaway: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.
learningObjective: Assess the meaning of preparatory or farewell communication.

title: A support person's role
stem: A client wants a sibling involved in a suicide safety plan. What should the nurse clarify?
options: That the sibling guarantees no future crisis
That professional follow-up is no longer needed
That the sibling should conceal every concern from clinicians
Agreed warning signs, practical actions and emergency contact routes
why: No support person can guarantee future safety.
Family support complements rather than replaces professional care.
Relevant safety concerns may require timely clinical communication.
Specific shared responsibilities make involvement useful and realistic.
takeaway: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.
learningObjective: Define concrete support roles without transferring all responsibility to family.

title: Crisis resources in Canada
stem: Which statements about a Canadian client's crisis-contact plan are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Call or text 9-8-8 for suicide crisis support
Use emergency services when immediate safety is at risk
Wait for office hours before contacting any service
Keep contact methods in a format the client can access
why: Canada's 9-8-8 service offers around-the-clock crisis support.
Immediate danger requires an emergency response.
Crisis needs may occur outside routine service hours.
Usability matters when concentration and coping are impaired.
takeaway: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.
learningObjective: Distinguish crisis support from emergency response and make contacts accessible.

title: Suicide risk after an acute loss
stem: A client lost housing yesterday, is intoxicated and says nothing matters. What should guide the nurse's response?
options: Wait for sobriety before providing any safety measures
Assess immediate safety and physical needs while arranging continued reassessment
Attribute the statement solely to alcohol
Focus only on housing paperwork until the client is calmer
why: Protective care should not be delayed while capacity to participate improves.
Intoxication and acute stress require immediate care plus reassessment over time.
Alcohol does not make suicidal statements clinically irrelevant.
Practical needs matter but do not replace immediate safety assessment.
takeaway: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.
learningObjective: Provide immediate safety care when intoxication limits a complete suicide assessment.

title: Risk documentation
stem: After a suicide-risk assessment, which documentation is most useful?
options: 'Client is safe' without supporting information
'Attention-seeking' as the main description
Relevant statements, observed cues, assessment findings and protective actions
Only the total score from a screening form
why: A broad label does not communicate evidence or limits.
A judgmental label obscures the actual clinical findings.
Specific evidence and actions support continuity and reassessment.
A score alone omits context and clinical judgment.
takeaway: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.
learningObjective: Document suicide-risk evidence and the actions taken.

title: Emerging mania
stem: A client with bipolar disorder has slept very little for three nights, feels unusually energetic and is spending impulsively. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange prompt clinical review of possible mood escalation
Praise improved energy without further assessment
Advise making major purchases while confidence is high
Wait for overt psychosis before contacting the team
why: Reduced sleep with impulsivity may signal a developing manic episode.
Increased energy can represent deterioration rather than recovery.
Major decisions may be impaired by mood elevation.
Earlier recognition allows intervention before more severe disruption.
takeaway: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced sleep and impulsivity as possible early mania.

title: Nutrition during mania
stem: A client experiencing mania paces continuously and leaves meals after a few bites. Which approach best supports intake?
options: Require sitting through a lengthy group meal
Focus exclusively on discussing food choices
Remove snacks to increase hunger at meals
Offer manageable nutritious foods and fluids with brief support
why: A long seated meal may exceed current concentration and activity tolerance.
Discussion alone does not improve actual intake.
Removing opportunities may worsen inadequate nutrition.
Accessible small offerings can fit the client's current behaviour.
takeaway: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.
learningObjective: Adapt nutrition support to the activity and attention patterns of mania.

title: Supporting sleep in mania
stem: Which nursing actions fit a coordinated plan for a client with acute mania? Select all that apply.
options: Reduce unnecessary evening stimulation
Monitor sleep and rest patterns
Encourage late-night competitive activities to tire the client
Provide predictable brief interactions
why: Lower stimulation supports an environment more compatible with rest.
Sleep trends inform severity and treatment response.
Competition and stimulation may intensify activation.
Predictable concise contact reduces overload and conflict.
takeaway: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.
learningObjective: Support rest through environmental adaptation and monitoring during mania.

title: Limit setting during mania
stem: A client with mania repeatedly enters other clients' rooms. What is the best nursing response?
options: Explain every policy in a lengthy lecture
State a brief clear boundary and redirect to an appropriate space
Ignore the behaviour until someone complains
Negotiate different privacy rules each time
why: Lengthy explanations may exceed current attention and escalate frustration.
Clear consistent limits protect others while giving a usable alternative.
Waiting permits continued intrusion and possible conflict.
Variable rules reduce predictability and effectiveness.
takeaway: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.
learningObjective: Use brief consistent boundaries with a concrete alternative during mania.

title: Impulsive financial decisions
stem: A hospitalized client with mania wants to make a large nonurgent purchase during marked distractibility. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete the transaction to preserve rapport
Decide the client's finances independently
Encourage postponement and involve the treatment team in assessing decision support needs
Ask another client to advise on the investment
why: Facilitating a major decision during impairment can increase harm.
Nurses do not automatically gain financial decision authority.
A pause and appropriate assessment protect autonomy and reduce impulsive harm.
Another client's opinion does not establish appropriate support.
takeaway: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.
learningObjective: Address impulsive high-impact decisions through delay and appropriate assessment.

title: Communication with pressured speech
stem: A client with mania speaks rapidly and changes topics before a question is completed. What approach is best?
options: Use brief concrete statements and gently return to the immediate topic
Match the client's speech speed and volume
Ask several questions together to save time
Explore multiple abstract themes simultaneously
why: Concise redirection supports comprehension despite distractibility.
Mirroring intensity may increase stimulation.
Multiple questions add cognitive load.
Abstract branching discussion may worsen disorganization.
takeaway: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.
learningObjective: Keep communication concrete and focused during manic distractibility.

title: Family plan for bipolar recurrence
stem: A client agrees to involve family in relapse prevention. What information is most useful?
options: A prediction that relapse cannot recur with support
A rule that every happy mood requires emergency care
A list of unrelated diagnostic terms
The client's early changes, agreed contacts and preferred support actions
why: Support reduces risk but cannot guarantee no recurrence.
Normal happiness is not equivalent to mania.
Vocabulary alone does not guide practical action.
Individualized early cues and responses make the plan actionable.
takeaway: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.
learningObjective: Build bipolar relapse plans around the client's own early warning pattern.

title: Evaluating mania improvement
stem: Which findings suggest improvement in a client treated for mania? Select all that apply.
options: Longer sustained sleep periods
Better ability to remain with a simple task
Increased impulsive spending plans
Improved food and fluid intake
why: Restoring sleep can indicate reduced activation.
Improved attention supports meaningful functional recovery.
Growing impulsivity suggests continuing impaired judgment.
Improved intake addresses a common physical consequence of mania.
takeaway: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate manic recovery through sleep, attention, judgment and basic needs.

title: Mood tracking for bipolar disorder
stem: A stable client wants to recognize recurrence earlier. Which tracking approach is most useful?
options: Record sleep, mood, activity and relevant triggers over time
Record only days that feel unusually positive
Use weight as the sole marker of mood stability
Ask family to infer the pattern without the client's input
why: Multiple daily patterns can reveal individualized early changes.
Selective entries may obscure depressive or mixed changes.
Weight alone does not describe mood recurrence.
The client's own experience is an important part of tracking.
takeaway: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.
learningObjective: Track mood alongside sleep, activity and context in bipolar care.

title: Feeling well and treatment continuation
stem: A stable client with bipolar disorder wants to stop follow-up because they feel well. What response best supports informed care?
options: Agree that follow-up is only useful during crises
Discuss maintenance goals and review concerns with the treating team
Tell the client recurrence is certain tomorrow
Focus only on past hospital costs
why: Maintenance care may support sustained stability and early recognition.
Collaborative review addresses preferences without abrupt unsupported changes.
An exact prediction is unjustified and fear-based.
Cost alone does not address the client's treatment question.
takeaway: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.
learningObjective: Explain the purpose of maintenance care during bipolar stability.

title: Depressive and activated symptoms together
stem: A client reports hopelessness while pacing, sleeping little and describing racing thoughts. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Assume increased energy means low suicide risk
Wait for a clearly elevated mood before review
Assess safety promptly and report the mixed symptom pattern
Focus only on bedtime routines
why: Energy and agitation can coexist with serious suicidal distress.
Clinically important activation need not appear as cheerful mood.
The combined pattern may create significant risk and needs clinical review.
Sleep advice alone is insufficient for this presentation.
takeaway: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.
learningObjective: Escalate hopelessness accompanied by activation or agitation.

title: Distinguishing reduced need from insomnia
stem: A client sleeps two hours and says they feel fully rested, unusually powerful and ready for major projects. What is most concerning?
options: Reduced sleep need with activation and grandiosity
The bedtime differs from the nurse's routine
The client prefers morning activity
The client recalls a vivid dream
why: The combined pattern suggests possible manic escalation requiring assessment.
Schedule differences alone do not establish a disorder.
Activity preference alone is not an acute warning sign.
Dream recall does not explain the activation pattern.
takeaway: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.
learningObjective: Assess reduced sleep need together with energy and judgment changes.

title: Protecting dignity during disinhibition
stem: A client with mania makes sexual comments toward peers. What should the nurse do?
options: Discuss the behaviour publicly to deter repetition
Ignore comments because they reflect illness
Encourage peers to confront the client as a group
Set respectful limits, redirect and assess the care plan
why: Public humiliation can escalate distress and damage dignity.
Illness does not remove the need to protect others' boundaries.
Group confrontation may intensify conflict.
Clear respectful intervention supports safety without shaming.
takeaway: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.
learningObjective: Address disinhibition with dignity, limits and coordinated reassessment.

title: Selecting manageable activities
stem: Which activities may fit a client whose mania is improving but who remains distractible? Select all that apply.
options: Brief simple tasks with staff support
Quiet noncompetitive activity with limited choices
A complex competitive tournament with many rules
Planned rest opportunities between activities
why: Simple supported tasks match limited sustained attention.
Lower stimulation reduces overload and competition-related escalation.
Complex competition may exceed attention and increase activation.
Rest opportunities support recovery from prolonged activation.
takeaway: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.
learningObjective: Match activity complexity and stimulation to current manic recovery.

title: Food-related suspiciousness
stem: A client with psychosis refuses meals because they fear tampering. They will accept intact packaged food. What is the best immediate nursing approach?
options: Argue that staff would never tamper with food
Offer acceptable sealed food while assessing intake and the belief's effect
Agree that ordinary meals are contaminated
Delay nutrition until the belief disappears
why: Argument may increase mistrust without improving intake.
An acceptable option supports nutrition without endorsing the belief.
Confirming contamination reinforces the delusional interpretation.
Waiting can worsen physical needs while symptoms persist.
takeaway: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.
learningObjective: Support basic needs without validating a delusion.

title: Thought blocking in conversation
stem: A client suddenly stops speaking mid-sentence and appears unable to continue. What should the nurse do?
options: Supply the likely ending immediately
Change topics several times to stimulate speech
Allow time and gently ask whether the client wants to continue
Interpret the pause as agreement with the nurse
why: Supplying content may distort the client's intended meaning.
Rapid topic changes add cognitive demands.
A patient pause supports communication without imposing an explanation.
Silence does not establish agreement.
takeaway: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.
learningObjective: Allow time and clarify sudden interruptions in thought.

title: Responding to unusual word meanings
stem: A client uses a word the nurse does not understand while describing distress. What is the best response?
options: Ask what that word means to the client
Pretend to understand to maintain rapport
Correct the vocabulary before assessing distress
Ask another client to translate the meaning
why: Clarification supports accurate understanding of the experience.
Pretending can lead to inaccurate assessment and care.
Language correction may distract from the clinical meaning.
Another client's interpretation cannot reliably replace clarification.
takeaway: Clarify unfamiliar language instead of assigning meaning.
learningObjective: Clarify unfamiliar language instead of assigning meaning.

title: Low initiation in schizophrenia
stem: A stable client with schizophrenia rarely begins hygiene tasks but participates when offered one-step prompts. What should the nurse do?
options: Label the client unwilling to cooperate
Withdraw prompts to test motivation
Provide long lists of tasks each morning
Use consistent manageable prompts and assess other contributors
why: Reduced initiation may reflect symptoms rather than deliberate refusal.
Removing effective support may worsen function.
Long lists may exceed attention or planning ability.
Structured support addresses function while considering depression or adverse effects.
takeaway: Support reduced initiation without assuming deliberate noncooperation.
learningObjective: Support reduced initiation without assuming deliberate noncooperation.

title: Assessing hallucination impact
stem: A client reports hearing voices. Which questions help determine the care needed? Select all that apply.
options: 'What do the voices say?'
'Do they tell you to do something?'
'Would proving they are unreal end this discussion?'
'How do they affect what you do?'
'Are you definitely ignoring them successfully?'
why: Content helps identify distress and safety implications.
Commands require further risk assessment.
Debate does not assess impact or coping.
Behavioural effects reveal functional and safety needs.
A leading assumption can conceal difficulty resisting voices.
takeaway: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.
learningObjective: Assess hallucination content, commands and behavioural effects.

title: Coping with noncommand voices
stem: A client hears distressing noncommand voices and identifies quiet music as helpful. What should the nurse do?
options: Require the same strategy for every client
Support the preferred strategy and reassess distress and safety
Tell the client to stop mentioning voices
Increase background sound regardless of preference
why: Coping responses differ among clients.
An effective chosen strategy can be integrated with ongoing assessment.
Suppressing disclosure undermines assessment and support.
More noise may increase distress rather than reduce it.
takeaway: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.
learningObjective: Evaluate individualized coping strategies for distressing hallucinations.

title: Psychosis and physical symptoms
stem: A client with chronic schizophrenia reports new abdominal pain and vomiting. What is the appropriate nursing response?
options: Attribute the report to delusional thinking
Delay assessment until the psychiatric review
Assess the physical symptoms and escalate findings appropriately
Ask whether hallucinations caused the pain before checking physical status
why: A psychiatric diagnosis does not exclude physical illness.
New symptoms may require timely medical evaluation.
Physical assessment prevents diagnostic overshadowing.
Symptom attribution should not delay basic clinical assessment.
takeaway: Investigate physical symptoms in clients with mental illness.
learningObjective: Investigate physical symptoms in clients with mental illness.

title: Distractibility during self-care teaching
stem: A client recovering from psychosis loses track during multistep instructions. What adaptation is best?
options: Teach one step at a time with practice
Repeat the full sequence more rapidly
Postpone every self-care activity until concentration is normal
Rely only on an extensive written manual
why: Single steps match current processing and allow feedback.
Faster delivery increases rather than reduces cognitive load.
Supported participation may be possible before full symptom resolution.
Lengthy reading may exceed the same cognitive capacity.
takeaway: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.
learningObjective: Break self-care learning into manageable steps during psychosis recovery.

title: Delusional fear of assessment
stem: A client believes a blood-pressure cuff can read thoughts and refuses it. No urgent measurement is needed. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply it quickly while the client is distracted
Agree that the cuff sometimes reads thoughts
Debate the belief until the client accepts the cuff
Acknowledge the fear, explain simply and explore an acceptable approach
why: Nonurgent care should not bypass refusal through surprise.
Agreement reinforces inaccurate device beliefs.
Extended argument may worsen mistrust.
A calm explanation and collaboration support trust without validating the belief.
takeaway: Address fear and negotiate nonurgent care without endorsing delusions.
learningObjective: Address fear and negotiate nonurgent care without endorsing delusions.

title: Early psychosis change
stem: Which changes in a young adult warrant timely mental-health assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Growing suspiciousness with decline in school function
New perceptual experiences causing distress
Choosing one quiet weekend after examinations
Using a written planner successfully for daily tasks
Preferring a different music genre
why: A sustained functional decline with suspiciousness is clinically meaningful.
Distressing altered perceptions need assessment and contextual review.
An isolated rest preference does not establish a disorder.
An effective organizational aid is adaptive and does not itself indicate emerging psychosis.
Taste differences alone are not a psychiatric warning sign.
takeaway: Assess emerging perceptual or thought changes that impair functioning.
learningObjective: Assess emerging perceptual or thought changes that impair functioning.

title: A belief and cultural context
stem: A client describes a spiritual experience unfamiliar to the nurse. What should the nurse do before interpreting it as psychosis?
options: Determine whether it matches the nurse's beliefs
Explore cultural meaning, distress, function and associated symptoms
Ask the family to reject the experience
Record a delusion solely because the belief is unfamiliar
why: Personal agreement is not a diagnostic standard.
Cultural context and clinical impact help avoid misinterpretation.
Rejection does not establish clinical meaning or safety.
Unfamiliarity alone is insufficient to label a belief delusional.
takeaway: Assess spiritual experiences within cultural and functional context.
learningObjective: Assess spiritual experiences within cultural and functional context.

title: Risk and diagnosis
stem: A staff member assumes a quiet client with schizophrenia is violent because of the diagnosis. What information should guide risk assessment?
options: The diagnostic label alone
Media portrayals of schizophrenia
Current behaviour, threats, distress, history and situational factors
Whether the client makes consistent eye contact
why: Diagnosis alone does not establish an individual's violence risk.
Media stereotypes are not clinical evidence.
Individualized evidence guides proportionate safety measures.
Eye contact alone is culturally variable and nonspecific.
takeaway: Assess behaviour and context rather than stereotyping psychiatric diagnosis.
learningObjective: Assess behaviour and context rather than stereotyping psychiatric diagnosis.

title: Suspiciousness during handoff
stem: A client becomes worried when two staff whisper nearby. What is the most useful change?
options: Communicate openly about relevant care in an appropriate private setting
Continue whispering and reassure only if asked
Ask the client to ignore all staff conversations
Explain every unrelated client's information to prove transparency
why: Clear relevant communication reduces avoidable ambiguity while preserving privacy.
Continued ambiguous behaviour may intensify mistrust.
Instruction to ignore concerns does not address the trigger.
Transparency does not justify disclosing others' information.
takeaway: Reduce avoidable ambiguity while preserving confidentiality.
learningObjective: Reduce avoidable ambiguity while preserving confidentiality.

title: A client stands motionless
stem: A client with a severe mood disorder remains motionless, barely responds and takes little food or fluid. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Assume the client is choosing solitude
Encourage a group activity before assessment
Wait until the next counselling session
Arrange prompt assessment of possible catatonia and physical compromise
why: Markedly reduced responsiveness may reflect a serious clinical syndrome.
Group participation does not address the immediate assessment need.
Delay can worsen hydration, nutrition and other complications.
The combined motor and intake changes warrant timely clinical review.
takeaway: Escalate marked motor withdrawal with reduced responsiveness or intake.
learningObjective: Escalate marked motor withdrawal with reduced responsiveness or intake.

title: Recovery goals in psychosis
stem: Which goals reflect a recovery-oriented plan for a client with persistent symptoms? Select all that apply.
options: Resuming a personally valued community activity
Developing a usable plan for distressing experiences
Requiring symptom elimination before discussing housing
Increasing choice and participation in daily decisions
Measuring success only by agreement with staff
why: Valued participation can be meaningful even with residual symptoms.
Practical coping supports function and safety.
Housing and other life needs should not await complete remission.
Choice and participation support self-determination.
Agreement alone does not establish recovery or wellbeing.
takeaway: Define recovery through the client's goals, agency and functioning.
learningObjective: Define recovery through the client's goals, agency and functioning.

title: Family education about hallucinations
stem: A caregiver asks how to respond when a relative reports voices. What should the nurse advise?
options: Pretend to hear the same voices
Acknowledge distress, avoid arguing and assess help needs
Demand proof before offering support
Discuss the voices with neighbours for reassurance
why: Pretending can validate the perceptual experience as shared reality.
Supportive reality-based communication preserves trust and identifies risk.
Demands for proof can increase isolation and distress.
Unnecessary disclosure undermines privacy.
takeaway: Teach family to acknowledge distress without confirming hallucinations.
learningObjective: Teach family to acknowledge distress without confirming hallucinations.

title: Daily function after psychosis
stem: A client wants to resume cooking but becomes distracted around a hot stove. What is the best plan?
options: Return immediately to complex meals alone
Stop all kitchen involvement indefinitely
Practise simpler tasks with appropriate support and review safety
Judge readiness solely by the absence of voices
why: Current distractibility creates a practical safety concern.
Permanent exclusion unnecessarily limits skill recovery.
Graded practice balances meaningful function and current ability.
Symptom presence alone does not describe task competence.
takeaway: Assess real-world task performance during psychosis recovery.
learningObjective: Assess real-world task performance during psychosis recovery.

title: Unwanted discussion of diagnosis
stem: A capable client does not want a visiting friend told about their psychosis diagnosis. What should the nurse do?
options: Respect the boundary while clarifying any agreed support involvement
Explain the diagnosis because visitors should understand
Ask the friend whether disclosure would be helpful
Treat accepting a visit as consent to share clinical details
why: A social visit does not remove the client's confidentiality preferences.
Helpful intent does not authorize disclosure.
The visitor cannot grant the client's permission.
Consent for contact is not equivalent to consent for health disclosure.
takeaway: Clarify consent before sharing mental-health information with visitors.
learningObjective: Clarify consent before sharing mental-health information with visitors.

title: Housing stability and recovery
stem: A client recovering from psychosis misses treatment because they move between shelters. What nursing action best addresses the problem?
options: Emphasize punctuality without reviewing access
Add a written appointment list only
Interpret missed visits as lack of insight alone
Coordinate practical contact and outreach options with the client's agreement
why: Punctuality advice does not resolve unstable access.
A list alone may not make care reachable.
Housing instability is an evident alternative explanation.
Flexible coordinated access can support continuity despite housing changes.
takeaway: Address housing-related barriers when planning mental-health follow-up.
learningObjective: Address housing-related barriers when planning mental-health follow-up.

title: Relapse planning after psychosis
stem: Which information is useful in a relapse-prevention plan? Select all that apply.
options: The client's own early warning changes
Agreed contacts and preferred responses
A guarantee that taking medication prevents every recurrence
Stressors and supports relevant to daily life
A rule that family should make every future decision
why: Personal patterns can improve early recognition.
Defined responses make warning signs actionable.
Treatment reduces risk but cannot guarantee no recurrence.
Context helps identify practical prevention and support opportunities.
Family involvement should not automatically replace client autonomy.
takeaway: Personalize relapse planning around warning signs, context and agreed responses.
learningObjective: Personalize relapse planning around warning signs, context and agreed responses.

title: Alcohol history before admission
stem: A client admitted for surgery reports daily heavy drinking and a previous withdrawal seizure. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Wait for tremor before informing the team
Communicate the history promptly for a monitored withdrawal-prevention plan
Advise stopping without further assessment
Focus only on postoperative pain education
why: A severe withdrawal history warrants planning before symptoms emerge.
Anticipatory assessment can reduce complications during forced interruption of use.
Unmonitored cessation can be dangerous in dependence.
Pain teaching does not address the identified withdrawal risk.
takeaway: Identify severe withdrawal history before alcohol use is interrupted.
learningObjective: Identify severe withdrawal history before alcohol use is interrupted.

title: Substance-use interviewing
stem: A client appears embarrassed when asked about alcohol intake. Which question is most likely to obtain useful information?
options: 'You do not drink too much, do you?'
'Why would you continue if it causes problems?'
'What do you usually drink, how much, and when was your last drink?'
'Can your family give us the real amount?'
why: A leading question invites minimization rather than detail.
Blame may reduce disclosure.
Neutral specific questions support assessment of pattern and withdrawal risk.
Collateral may help but should not presume the client's account is false.
takeaway: Ask neutral specific questions about substance use.
learningObjective: Ask neutral specific questions about substance use.

title: Intoxication and an injury history
stem: A drowsy client who smells of alcohol arrives after an unwitnessed fall. Which action takes priority?
options: Assess airway, neurologic status and possible injury promptly
Obtain a detailed account of usual drinking patterns first
Arrange transport home once a relative answers the phone
Recheck alertness after an uninterrupted period of sleep
why: Intoxication can coexist with serious injury and must not explain away reduced responsiveness.
Substance history is useful but does not precede immediate physical assessment.
A ride home does not establish medical stability after a fall.
Waiting for sleep can delay recognition of injury or airway compromise.
takeaway: Assess injury and physiologic stability before attributing drowsiness to alcohol.
learningObjective: Assess injury and physiologic stability before attributing drowsiness to alcohol.

title: Withdrawal and a scoring tool
stem: A nurse obtains a withdrawal severity score that has risen since the previous assessment. What is the best next step?
options: Record the number and wait until the next shift
Use the score without considering vital signs or behaviour
Change medication independently beyond the authorized plan
Apply the approved protocol and communicate worsening clinical findings
why: A worsening score requires timely response, not documentation alone.
Tools supplement rather than replace clinical assessment.
Medication changes must follow appropriate authority and orders.
Protocol-guided response combines measurement with clinical judgment.
takeaway: Respond to worsening withdrawal using both clinical assessment and authorized protocols.
learningObjective: Respond to worsening withdrawal using both clinical assessment and authorized protocols.

title: Severe withdrawal warning findings
stem: During alcohol withdrawal monitoring, which changes require urgent escalation? Select all that apply.
options: New disorientation with marked agitation
A generalized seizure
Mild hunger after a tolerated meal
Mild stable hand tremor without other deterioration
Requesting information about later treatment
why: Disorientation can indicate severe complicated withdrawal.
A seizure requires immediate emergency assessment and management.
Appetite return alone is not a severe withdrawal sign.
Mild stable tremor requires monitoring but does not carry the urgency of a seizure or new disorientation.
Interest in treatment is not itself acute deterioration.
takeaway: Escalate neurologic changes and marked instability during alcohol withdrawal.
learningObjective: Escalate neurologic changes and marked instability during alcohol withdrawal.

title: Withdrawal recovery versus addiction treatment
stem: After medically supervised withdrawal, a client says, 'The problem is cured now.' What should the nurse explain?
options: Withdrawal treatment and longer-term recovery support serve different needs
No further assessment is ever needed after detoxification
Cravings prove the withdrawal treatment failed completely
Only inpatient care can support future recovery
why: Stabilization does not automatically address ongoing use patterns and relapse risks.
Continued support may be important after acute symptoms resolve.
Cravings can persist and should guide the ongoing plan.
Recovery services can be provided in several settings.
takeaway: Link withdrawal stabilization with ongoing treatment and recovery planning.
learningObjective: Link withdrawal stabilization with ongoing treatment and recovery planning.

title: A return to drinking
stem: A client resumed drinking after several months of abstinence and avoids follow-up out of shame. What response best supports re-engagement?
options: Require a period of abstinence before another appointment
Assess current safety and explore what preceded the return to use
Treat the event as proof treatment cannot work
Focus only on whether the client disappointed relatives
why: Delaying access can worsen harm during a vulnerable period.
Current risk and triggers guide a constructive revised plan.
Recurrence does not mean future treatment is futile.
Family disappointment does not substitute for clinical assessment.
takeaway: Use recurrence to reassess safety, triggers and support needs.
learningObjective: Use recurrence to reassess safety, triggers and support needs.

title: Alcohol and sedating medication
stem: A client takes a prescribed sedative and drinks alcohol to help sleep. What should the nurse prioritize in teaching?
options: Take both earlier in the evening
Use beverage type to decide safety
Discuss additive sedation and arrange medication and alcohol review
Skip the medication whenever alcohol is available without consulting the plan
why: Earlier timing does not remove combined depressant effects.
Alcohol content and drug effects matter more than beverage category.
Combined sedation can increase serious impairment and needs individualized review.
Unsupervised changes may create additional treatment or withdrawal risks.
takeaway: Assess and address combined depressant exposure.
learningObjective: Assess and address combined depressant exposure.

title: Exploring readiness for change
stem: A client says reducing alcohol might improve family life but doubts they can manage stress. What response is most useful?
options: Explore desired changes and alternative ways to manage stress
List consequences until the client promises abstinence
Avoid the topic until the client is fully certain
Choose a goal on the client's behalf
why: Exploring values and coping barriers supports collaborative change.
Pressure may produce agreement without readiness or a feasible plan.
Ambivalence can be explored rather than waiting passively.
Imposed goals may not match motivation or capacity.
takeaway: Explore the benefits and barriers the client identifies in changing substance use.
learningObjective: Explore the benefits and barriers the client identifies in changing substance use.

title: Recovery and meaningful routines
stem: A client in early recovery reports that evenings previously centred on substance use now feel empty. What should the nurse help plan?
options: Avoid every evening social contact
Fill every hour with compulsory tasks
Resume the previous routine without examining triggers
Feasible valued activities and supportive contacts during high-risk times
why: Isolation may reduce protective social connection.
An overloaded imposed plan may be unsustainable.
Previous routines may contain important use cues.
Purposeful alternatives address the specific time and function of use.
takeaway: Plan meaningful alternatives for times previously organized around substance use.
learningObjective: Plan meaningful alternatives for times previously organized around substance use.

title: Respectful substance-use documentation
stem: Which entries are clinically useful and nonstigmatizing? Select all that apply.
options: 'Reports using opioids yesterday; last use at approximately 20:00.'
'Declined the offered referral after discussing options.'
'Drug-seeking and manipulative' without behavioural details
'Requests pain review; rates pain and describes its location.'
'Noncompliant addict' as the summary assessment
why: Specific timing supports assessment without a character judgment.
The entry documents a decision and relevant process.
Labels obscure observable findings and can bias care.
Descriptive assessment supports appropriate evaluation.
Stigmatizing language does not explain the clinical situation.
takeaway: Document substance-use information and behaviour without judgmental labels.
learningObjective: Document substance-use information and behaviour without judgmental labels.

title: Pain with opioid-use disorder
stem: A client receiving treatment for opioid-use disorder reports postoperative pain. What should the nurse do?
options: Assume the report is solely a request for drugs
Assess pain and coordinate an appropriate plan with the treating team
Withhold discussion until the client proves abstinence
Ask peers to judge whether the pain is believable
why: A substance-use diagnosis does not exclude genuine pain.
Pain and addiction treatment require coordinated individualized care.
Care should not depend on an arbitrary proof requirement.
Peer opinion is not a clinical pain assessment.
takeaway: Assess and treat pain without diagnostic stigma.
learningObjective: Assess and treat pain without diagnostic stigma.

title: Naloxone follow-up teaching
stem: A client's family learns to use take-home naloxone. Which additional message is essential?
options: Recovery after naloxone means emergency assessment is unnecessary
Naloxone permanently removes all opioid effects
Call emergency help and continue monitoring because effects can recur
Save naloxone only for people with a confirmed prescription
why: Initial improvement may be temporary.
Naloxone's effect may wear off before the opioid's effect.
Emergency response and ongoing observation remain necessary after administration.
Suspected opioid poisoning warrants response regardless of prescription status.
takeaway: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.
learningObjective: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.

title: Lower tolerance after abstinence
stem: A client leaving treatment asks about returning to a previous opioid amount after weeks without use. What should the nurse explain?
options: Reduced tolerance can increase overdose risk; discuss prevention and treatment supports
The previously tolerated amount remains equally safe
Only the source of the opioid changes risk
Tolerance always returns before harmful effects occur
why: Abstinence can reduce tolerance, making recurrence particularly hazardous.
Past tolerance does not establish present safety.
Dose, tolerance, combinations and supply can all affect risk.
There is no assurance tolerance returns before toxicity.
takeaway: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.
learningObjective: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.

title: Mixed-drug overdose concern
stem: A family asks whether to withhold naloxone if an unresponsive person's substance exposure is uncertain. What should teaching emphasize?
options: Wait for proof of an opioid before calling help
Use naloxone instead of contacting emergency services
Assume naloxone reverses every sedating substance
Follow emergency response guidance and use naloxone when opioid poisoning is suspected
why: Waiting can delay lifesaving response.
Naloxone does not replace emergency care and supportive measures.
Nonopioid effects may persist even when opioids are reversed.
Suspected opioid involvement warrants prompt response despite incomplete information.
takeaway: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.
learningObjective: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.

title: Preparing an overdose prevention plan
stem: Which topics should be included when a client may return to nonprescribed opioid use? Select all that apply.
options: Access to naloxone and knowing how to use it
Lower tolerance after a period without use
Assuming familiar packaging guarantees drug contents
Available local overdose-prevention and treatment services
Avoiding discussion unless the client promises abstinence
why: Ready access and training support a timely response.
Tolerance changes are an important overdose risk.
Appearance or packaging cannot establish contents or potency.
Local services can provide prevention and treatment support.
Harm-reduction discussion should not depend on an abstinence promise.
takeaway: Provide practical overdose prevention alongside treatment options.
learningObjective: Provide practical overdose prevention alongside treatment options.

title: Opioid withdrawal distress
stem: A client with opioid dependence develops yawning, diffuse aches, diarrhea and restlessness after interruption of use. What is the best response?
options: Treat distress as misconduct before assessment
Assess withdrawal, hydration and treatment needs without judgment
Assume every symptom is an overdose
Require counselling participation before addressing physical symptoms
why: Behavioural blame can delay needed physical care.
Symptom assessment supports appropriate treatment and engagement.
Withdrawal and overdose patterns differ and require assessment.
Physical needs should not be conditional on counselling participation.
takeaway: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.
learningObjective: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.

title: Stimulant-related acute symptoms
stem: A client reports recent stimulant use and now has chest pain, severe agitation and overheating. What is the priority?
options: Begin a detailed relapse-prevention interview
Encourage vigorous movement to release tension
Arrange emergency physical assessment and maintain a safe low-stimulation setting
Wait for sleep to resolve the symptoms
why: Counselling is secondary to possible acute medical toxicity.
Exertion may worsen overheating and cardiovascular strain.
These symptoms can signal serious toxicity requiring urgent care.
Waiting risks deterioration from potentially life-threatening complications.
takeaway: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.
learningObjective: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.

title: Cannabis-related anxiety
stem: A client develops marked anxiety and suspiciousness after a high-potency cannabis product. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess exposure, physical status and safety in a calm setting
Assume legalization means the symptoms are unrelated
Debate every suspicious statement before assessment
Recommend another dose to establish tolerance
why: Assessment addresses intoxication, possible complications and immediate support needs.
Legal availability does not eliminate adverse effects.
Argument can worsen distress and delay evaluation.
Additional exposure may intensify symptoms.
takeaway: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.
learningObjective: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.

title: Concurrent mental-health and substance needs
stem: A client with depression drinks to manage distress and is told to address only one condition first. What plan is more appropriate?
options: Defer all mood care until permanent abstinence
Defer all alcohol assessment until mood completely resolves
Refer separately without communication between services
Coordinate assessment and support for both interacting concerns
why: Delaying mood care may leave a driver of distress untreated.
Alcohol-related risks need assessment even while depression is treated.
Fragmentation may miss interactions and create conflicting plans.
Integrated care addresses the overlapping clinical and practical needs.
takeaway: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.
learningObjective: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.

title: Evaluating recovery support
stem: Which outcomes indicate useful progress in a client's substance-use recovery plan? Select all that apply.
options: Earlier help-seeking when cravings increase
Improved participation in valued daily roles
Willingness to agree with every staff opinion
Reduced harmful use patterns according to the agreed goals
Avoiding appointments to prevent embarrassment
why: Timely help-seeking demonstrates use of support before escalation.
Recovery includes meaningful functioning and participation.
Agreement alone does not establish clinical progress.
Outcomes should reflect the collaboratively defined harm and use targets.
Missed care may reduce support during difficulties.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.

title: Gambling-related financial distress
stem: A client reports chasing gambling losses and hiding debt from family. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Preferred game and expected winning strategy
Immediate safety, financial harm, control over gambling and available supports
Whether the client can win enough to repay the debt
Only the family's opinion of gambling

Gambling-related distress can include serious financial and suicide risks.
Further gambling may increase rather than resolve harm.

takeaway: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.
learningObjective: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.

title: Problematic gaming and function
stem: A student games late into the night and repeatedly misses classes but denies any difficulty. What should the nurse explore?
options: Whether the game is currently popular
Whether parents dislike technology
Sleep, control over use, missed responsibilities and the student's goals
Whether the device is expensive
why: Popularity does not determine functional impact.
Family attitudes do not replace assessment of the student's experience.
Function and control distinguish a preferred activity from a harmful pattern.
Price does not establish severity or support needs.
takeaway: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.
learningObjective: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.

title: Family boundaries during recovery
stem: A parent asks whether paying every gambling debt will protect their adult child. What should the nurse do?
options: Explore boundaries and support options without taking over family decisions
Instruct the parent to pay all debts immediately
Recommend ending every relationship with the client
Focus only on the interest rate of the debt
why: Collaborative discussion can address support, safety and enabling patterns.
Automatic payment may not address the underlying harmful behaviour.
Complete cutoff is not a universal therapeutic requirement.
Financial details alone miss the family and behavioural issues.
takeaway: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.
learningObjective: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.

title: Choosing peer support
stem: A client wants recovery support but felt uncomfortable in a previous group. What is the best response?
options: Insist that one group is the only effective option
Interpret discomfort as proof of low motivation
Stop discussing peer support entirely
Explore what did not fit and offer suitable alternatives
why: Recovery supports differ in approach and fit.
Discomfort may reflect format, accessibility or preference.
One poor fit does not exclude all peer support.
Tailored alternatives support informed engagement.
takeaway: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.
learningObjective: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.

title: Planning after a substance-related admission
stem: Which discharge details require clarification for a client entering community treatment? Select all that apply.
options: How the first appointment will be reached
Who will address urgent withdrawal or recurrence concerns
Whether a referral name alone proves treatment has started
How prescribed treatment will continue without an access gap
Whether the client can promise never to have cravings
why: Transport and access determine whether follow-up is feasible.
Clear urgent contacts support timely response to deterioration.
Referral issuance does not confirm connection to care.
Treatment continuity can prevent avoidable destabilization.
Cravings cannot be eliminated by a promise.
takeaway: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.
learningObjective: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.

title: Strengths in mental-health recovery
stem: A client says the only meaningful goal is returning to caring for a garden. Which plan best reflects recovery-oriented care?
options: Replace the goal with a standard ward target
Link treatment and supports to gradual return to gardening
Require complete symptom absence before discussing it
Use staff convenience to decide the final goal
why: Standard targets may miss the client's motivation and values.
A valued role can organize meaningful recovery steps.
Participation can improve before every symptom disappears.
Service routines should not define the client's personal recovery.
takeaway: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.
learningObjective: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.

title: Supported employment goal
stem: A client recovering from severe mental illness wants to work but fears disclosing the diagnosis. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell the client to disclose to every coworker
Discourage employment until confidence is perfect
Explore goals and connect with appropriate vocational and disclosure advice
Choose the employer without involving the client
why: Disclosure decisions are individualized and involve privacy considerations.
Supported work planning need not wait for perfect confidence.
Specialist support can address function, accommodations and informed choice.
The client's preferences and participation are central.
takeaway: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.
learningObjective: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.

title: Self-stigma after diagnosis
stem: A client says, 'Having a mental illness means I cannot be a good parent.' What response is best?
options: Explore the concern and identify parenting strengths and support needs
Agree that diagnosis determines parenting ability
Offer reassurance without discussing actual functioning
Ask relatives to judge the client's worth as a parent
why: Function, strengths and needed support are more informative than a label.
Diagnosis alone does not determine parenting capacity.
Unsupported reassurance may miss real concerns or helpful resources.
Worth judgments do not provide a clinical assessment.
takeaway: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.
learningObjective: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.

title: Shared decisions in recovery
stem: A client finds the current treatment plan burdensome and wants changes. They are stable and capable of participating. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that stability removes the need to discuss concerns
Change all treatments independently
Ask family to overrule the client's preferences
Clarify burdens and goals and arrange collaborative treatment review
why: Burden can affect sustainability even when symptoms are stable.
Changes require appropriate authority and clinical coordination.
Family preference does not replace capable participation.
Shared review balances preferences, benefits, risks and feasible options.
takeaway: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.
learningObjective: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.

title: Measuring community recovery
stem: Which indicators can help evaluate a community mental-health plan? Select all that apply.
options: Progress toward the client's chosen housing or activity goals
Access to support when early difficulties appear
Absence of any disagreement with clinicians
The client's sense of choice and participation
Number of pamphlets provided as the sole outcome
why: Personal goals reflect meaningful life outcomes.
Usable support can prevent avoidable crises.
Agreement does not establish recovery or quality of care.
Agency is an important recovery-oriented outcome.
Materials distributed do not demonstrate benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.

title: Grief around an anniversary
stem: A client functioning well after a partner's death becomes tearful near the anniversary. What is the best response?
options: Reassess supports and discuss what this date means to the client
Conclude the earlier recovery was not real
Advise cancelling every remembrance activity
Focus on how many months grief should last
why: Anniversary reactions can renew grief and benefit from individualized support.
Renewed emotion does not erase previous adaptation.
Remembrance preferences differ and should be explored.
A fixed timetable does not describe an individual's grief.
takeaway: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.
learningObjective: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.

title: Anticipatory grief
stem: A spouse caring for a terminally ill partner says, 'I already miss our old life, even though they are alive.' What should the nurse say?
options: 'Focus on being grateful they are still here.'
'You are grieving changes and losses that are happening now.'
'Save these feelings for after the death.'
'This means you are ready to stop caring for them.'
why: Gratitude framing can suppress valid feelings of loss.
Anticipatory grief can occur before death and include current changes.
Emotional support is appropriate before as well as after death.
Grief does not establish a wish to abandon caregiving.
takeaway: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.
learningObjective: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.

title: Grieving different ways
stem: After a child's death, one parent wants to talk and the other prefers quiet activity. Both remain engaged in daily life. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: The quieter parent is necessarily avoiding grief
Both parents should use identical coping methods
Different expressions can be valid; explore how each wants support
The more tearful parent has the more serious loss
why: Quiet coping does not by itself establish pathological avoidance.
Grief expression differs among individuals.
Mutual understanding can support both people without ranking responses.
Visible emotion does not measure the importance of the loss.
takeaway: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.
learningObjective: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.

title: A child asks about death
stem: A young child asks why a deceased grandparent will not wake up. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Say the grandparent is sleeping deeply
Explain the entire organ-failure sequence
Change the topic to protect the child
Use simple direct language that the body stopped working and cannot wake
why: Sleep language can confuse death with normal sleep.
Technical detail may exceed the child's developmental needs.
Avoidance leaves the child's question and possible fears unresolved.
Concrete honest language supports understanding without confusing euphemisms.
takeaway: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.
learningObjective: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.

title: Grief requiring further assessment
stem: Which findings in a bereaved client warrant additional clinical assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Persistent inability to meet basic needs
Suicidal thoughts with intent
Occasional tears while discussing memories
Marked sustained functional deterioration
Choosing a culturally meaningful mourning practice
why: Basic self-care failure can create immediate health needs.
Intent requires prompt safety assessment.
Tearfulness alone can occur during adaptive grieving.
Sustained impairment may require additional support or treatment.
Cultural practices should not be pathologized without context.
takeaway: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.
learningObjective: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.

title: An unrecognized loss
stem: A client grieves the death of a former partner, but relatives say the relationship should no longer matter. What is the best nursing response?
options: Focus only on relatives with current legal relationships
Acknowledge the client's loss and ask what support would help
Advise avoiding mention of the relationship
Determine whether the family approves before offering support
why: Emotional significance is not determined solely by formal relationship status.
Recognizing the loss supports someone whose grief is socially minimized.
Silence may deepen isolation.
Family approval is not required to acknowledge distress.
takeaway: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.
learningObjective: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.

title: Offering remembrance choices
stem: After a pregnancy loss, a client is unsure about keepsakes or seeing the infant. What should the nurse do?
options: Select keepsakes based on the nurse's preferences
Interpret hesitation as refusal of every option
Explain available choices gently and allow the client to decide
Ask relatives to select the keepsakes to spare the client decisions
why: Personal preferences should not replace the client's decisions.
Hesitation may reflect a need for information or time.
Sensitive choices support control during loss without pressure.
Relatives may support decisions but should not automatically replace the client's preferences.
takeaway: Offer bereavement choices without assuming what will be meaningful.
learningObjective: Offer bereavement choices without assuming what will be meaningful.

title: Guilt after a death
stem: A client says, 'If I had called sooner, my parent would still be alive.' The cause and preventability are uncertain. What should the nurse say?
options: 'You are carrying a lot of guilt; tell me what you are thinking.'
'You definitely could not have changed anything.'
'You should stop thinking about the timing.'
'Your family can decide whether you were responsible.'
why: Exploration acknowledges emotion without making unsupported factual claims.
Absolute reassurance is not supported by the available information.
Thought suppression does not address the client's concern.
Blame assignment is not a therapeutic grief intervention.
takeaway: Explore bereavement guilt without unsupported promises or judgments.
learningObjective: Explore bereavement guilt without unsupported promises or judgments.

title: Grief and practical needs
stem: A recently bereaved client is overwhelmed by meals, appointments and paperwork. What should the nurse do first?
options: Provide a complete long-term grief reading list
Ask the client to complete every task independently
Focus exclusively on emotional expression
Help identify the most urgent practical needs and available support
why: Extensive reading may increase rather than reduce immediate overload.
Independence should not be imposed when support is needed.
Practical burdens can worsen distress and also need attention.
Prioritization makes immediate coping and assistance more feasible.
takeaway: Address practical burdens alongside emotional needs during bereavement.
learningObjective: Address practical burdens alongside emotional needs during bereavement.

title: Supporting a mourning ritual
stem: Which actions support culturally respectful bereavement care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask which practices matter to this family
Explore feasible accommodation of requested rituals
Infer every preference from ethnicity
Explain constraints transparently and seek acceptable alternatives
Apply the nurse's own religious practices by default
why: Direct inquiry avoids stereotyping individual preferences.
Accommodation can support meaning and comfort.
Shared identity does not determine every family's practices.
Collaborative alternatives preserve respect when constraints exist.
The family's values should guide spiritual support.
takeaway: Ask about mourning practices and collaborate on respectful accommodation.
learningObjective: Ask about mourning practices and collaborate on respectful accommodation.

title: Caregiver overload
stem: A spouse caring for a person with dementia reports sleeping poorly, missing meals and feeling trapped. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Explore care demands, wellbeing, safety and feasible respite
Remind the spouse of the original marriage commitment
Provide only a dementia fact sheet
Ask the spouse to wait until the next crisis before requesting help
why: Assessment can identify burnout, health risks and practical relief.
