Information alone does not address exhaustion and unmet needs.
Earlier support may prevent harm and care breakdown.
takeaway: Assess caregiver health and support before exhaustion becomes a crisis.
learningObjective: Assess caregiver health and support before exhaustion becomes a crisis.

title: Family role changes after illness
stem: A client cannot resume previous household responsibilities after an injury and feels useless. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Assign every former task back immediately
Explore valued roles and negotiate achievable contributions with the family
Recommend withdrawing from household decisions
Focus only on the family's lost productivity
why: Immediate full demands may exceed current ability.
Adapted meaningful roles support identity and participation during recovery.
Exclusion can intensify powerlessness.
Productivity alone does not capture emotional and relational needs.
takeaway: Support meaningful role adaptation after illness or disability.
learningObjective: Support meaningful role adaptation after illness or disability.

title: Adult client and family disagreement
stem: A capable client wants less family involvement in counselling than relatives prefer. What should guide the nurse's plan?
options: The relative who provides the most financial support
The largest number of family votes
The client's preferences and agreed limits on involvement
The nurse's preferred family structure
why: Financial support does not automatically confer decision authority.
A majority vote does not replace capable consent.
Client-defined boundaries guide legitimate family participation.
Personal assumptions should not determine the client's support network.
takeaway: Negotiate family involvement with the capable client's consent.
learningObjective: Negotiate family involvement with the capable client's consent.

title: A family requests secrecy
stem: Relatives ask the nurse not to tell a capable adult that a serious diagnosis was confirmed. What is the best next response?
options: Promise secrecy before meeting the client
Give all details to relatives for them to control
Assume cultural background establishes the client's wishes
Explore concerns and clarify the client's own information preferences with the team
why: A promise may conflict with the client's right to participate.
Family gatekeeping does not automatically reflect the client's preferences.
Culture should be explored individually rather than presumed.
Clarifying preferences supports respectful informed communication.
takeaway: Explore family concerns while establishing the client's own information wishes.
learningObjective: Explore family concerns while establishing the client's own information wishes.

title: Family assessment after a crisis
stem: Which questions help assess a family's coping resources? Select all that apply.
options: 'Who helps when responsibilities become difficult?'
'How have you managed major changes before?'
'Which person is to blame for the current stress?'
'What support would make the next few days manageable?'
'Can you prove your family never disagrees?'
why: Available help identifies practical and emotional resources.
Previous coping can reveal strengths and limitations.
Blame does not establish useful coping capacity.
Immediate priorities guide achievable support.
Absence of disagreement is not a realistic measure of coping.
takeaway: Assess support, previous coping and immediate practical needs in families.
learningObjective: Assess support, previous coping and immediate practical needs in families.

title: Partner violence and readiness
stem: A client discloses partner violence but is not ready to leave. They are currently in a private safe setting. What should the nurse do?
options: Require leaving before further support is offered
Assess danger and collaborate on a safety plan and accessible resources
Contact the partner to negotiate reconciliation
Describe staying as consent to further violence
why: Conditional support may increase isolation and reduce future help-seeking.
Safety planning can help even when the client is not ready to leave.
Partner contact may increase risk and is not an automatic nursing intervention.
Responsibility for violence rests with the person using it.
takeaway: Offer safety planning without requiring an immediate decision to leave.
learningObjective: Offer safety planning without requiring an immediate decision to leave.

title: Digital safety after violence
stem: A client experiencing partner violence says their phone is monitored. What should the nurse consider before sending resources?
options: Send a clearly labelled violence-service message immediately
Assume a private browser always removes every trace
Ask about a safe communication method and resource format
Ask the partner which method is acceptable
why: Visible messages may expose help-seeking and increase danger.
Digital privacy cannot be guaranteed from browser settings alone.
Client-informed communication planning reduces foreseeable disclosure risk.
Involving the partner may compromise safety and control.
takeaway: Check communication safety before sharing violence-related resources.
learningObjective: Check communication safety before sharing violence-related resources.

title: Disclosure of coercive control
stem: A client says a partner controls money and prevents medical appointments but has never hit them. What should the nurse recognize?
options: Coercive control can be harmful even without physical assault
Absence of injuries excludes partner violence
Financial decisions are outside any relevant nursing assessment
Medical access is adequate if the partner approves occasional visits
why: Control over resources and care can undermine safety and autonomy.
Violence and abuse can include nonphysical forms.
Financial control can directly obstruct health and safety.
Restricted access can remain harmful despite occasional permission.
takeaway: Assess controlling behaviours that restrict autonomy and health-care access.
learningObjective: Assess controlling behaviours that restrict autonomy and health-care access.

title: Responding to an assault disclosure
stem: After receiving urgent physical care, an adult survivor says they are unsure about contacting police. What should the nurse do?
options: Promise that reporting is never required under any circumstance
Contact police automatically without reviewing the situation
Advise against reporting to reduce stress
Explain available options, applicable limits and support informed choices
why: Reporting duties can depend on law and circumstances.
Automatic action may disregard consent or the applicable legal context.
The nurse should not impose a decision against reporting.
Clear information and support preserve agency while respecting requirements.
takeaway: Support informed choices after assault within applicable reporting requirements.
learningObjective: Support informed choices after assault within applicable reporting requirements.

title: Possible financial exploitation
stem: An older adult says a relative uses their bank card and leaves too little money for food. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Speak privately about the arrangement and the client's wishes
Assess immediate needs and decision-making context
Assume family involvement makes the arrangement acceptable
Offer appropriate safeguarding and community resources
Publicly accuse the relative before clarifying events
why: A private account can clarify consent, control and concerns.
Food access and current safety may require prompt support.
Family status does not establish that use is consensual or safe.
Resources can support protection and informed options.
Premature confrontation can increase risk and hinder assessment.
takeaway: Assess suspected exploitation privately and address immediate needs.
learningObjective: Assess suspected exploitation privately and address immediate needs.

title: Dementia and distress during bathing
stem: A client with dementia becomes frightened when rushed into a shower but tolerates familiar routines. What should the nurse try?
options: A slower familiar approach with simple explanations and choices
Several staff giving instructions simultaneously
Finishing quickly while ignoring fear
Requiring a shower at the same time regardless of response
why: Familiar pacing can reduce threat and preserve participation.
Multiple voices may increase confusion and overload.
Ignoring distress can escalate resistance and harm trust.
Rigid timing may conflict with individual comfort and needs.
takeaway: Adapt personal care to the person's dementia-related distress cues.
learningObjective: Adapt personal care to the person's dementia-related distress cues.

title: A repeated accusation in dementia
stem: A client with dementia says their purse was stolen; it is safely stored nearby. What is the best response?
options: Insist the client admit forgetting
Acknowledge the worry and help locate the purse
Explain memory pathology in a lengthy lecture
Ask the client to prove a theft occurred
why: Confrontation may increase distress without restoring recall.
Responding to the underlying concern can provide reassurance and resolution.
Detailed explanation may exceed current processing capacity.
Demands for proof do not address the immediate insecurity.
takeaway: Respond to the concern beneath dementia-related accusations.
learningObjective: Respond to the concern beneath dementia-related accusations.

title: Sudden withdrawal in dementia
stem: A normally interactive resident with dementia becomes unusually quiet and inattentive over one shift. What should the nurse do?
options: Interpret quietness as improvement in behaviour
Wait for agitation before assessing change
Assess for acute illness or delirium and report the change
Arrange routine memory testing at the next monthly review
why: Reduced activity can reflect hypoactive delirium rather than improvement.
Delirium need not present with agitation.
Acute deviation from baseline requires clinical evaluation.
Routine testing later would delay evaluation of an acute change.
takeaway: Recognize quiet acute cognitive change as potentially serious.
learningObjective: Recognize quiet acute cognitive change as potentially serious.

title: Pain-related behaviour in dementia
stem: A nonverbal client with dementia grimaces and resists turning after a fall. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Treat resistance as a personality issue
Use distraction before examining for injury
Increase commands to improve cooperation
Assess pain and possible injury using appropriate observational methods
why: The new behaviour has a plausible physical trigger.
Distraction may help comfort but does not replace injury assessment.
More commands can increase distress without addressing pain.
Behavioural cues may be the client's main expression of pain.
takeaway: Assess pain and injury when behaviour changes in a nonverbal client.
learningObjective: Assess pain and injury when behaviour changes in a nonverbal client.

title: Supporting orientation in delirium
stem: Which interventions may support a client with delirium while causes are treated? Select all that apply.
options: Provide calm repeated orientation as tolerated
Ensure needed hearing and visual aids are available
Keep the room continuously dark to reduce all stimulation
Encourage familiar supportive contact where appropriate
Challenge each mistaken statement until the client agrees
why: Gentle orientation can support connection to the current setting.
Sensory access reduces avoidable misinterpretation and isolation.
Continuous darkness can worsen sleep-wake disruption and disorientation.
Familiar presence may reduce fear and support orientation.
Repeated confrontation can increase distress without correcting delirium.
takeaway: Support orientation and sensory access alongside treatment of delirium causes.
learningObjective: Support orientation and sensory access alongside treatment of delirium causes.

title: Wandering with a purpose
stem: A resident with dementia walks repeatedly toward the exit each afternoon and says they must collect their children. What should the nurse explore?
options: A familiar routine or unmet need underlying the behaviour
Whether punishment would reduce walking
A restraint order before assessing patterns
Whether the resident can recite the current year first
why: Timing and stated purpose can guide individualized redirection and safety support.
Punishment does not address cognitive impairment or unmet needs.
Restriction should not replace assessment and less restrictive approaches.
Orientation testing alone does not explain the walking pattern.
takeaway: Look for patterns and meaning in dementia-related walking.
learningObjective: Look for patterns and meaning in dementia-related walking.

title: Care choices with cognitive impairment
stem: A client with dementia can choose between two outfits but struggles with complex decisions. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove all choices because dementia is diagnosed
Offer simple meaningful choices within the client's ability
Ask relatives to choose every daily preference
Use complex choices to test the client repeatedly
why: A diagnosis does not eliminate every form of participation.
Adapted choices preserve autonomy and dignity.
Relatives can support care without replacing all personal preference.
Repeated overload can create unnecessary distress.
takeaway: Preserve decision participation appropriate to the person's ability.
learningObjective: Preserve decision participation appropriate to the person's ability.

title: Unexpected touch and aggression
stem: A resident with dementia pushes a caregiver who approaches from behind. What preventive change is most useful?
options: Increase caregiver speed during future care
Use louder instructions from behind
Approach within view, identify oneself and explain the next step
Avoid every physical-care task afterward
why: Speed may increase surprise and perceived threat.
Loud unexpected commands can intensify distress.
Predictable visible approach reduces avoidable startle and confusion.
Necessary care can often continue with adaptation.
takeaway: Reduce surprise and perceived threat during dementia care.
learningObjective: Reduce surprise and perceived threat during dementia care.

title: Family expects memory recovery
stem: A family repeatedly quizzes a client with dementia and becomes frustrated by incorrect answers. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Increase quiz frequency to strengthen effort
Correct every mistake publicly
Compare performance with previous visits during meals
Use supportive conversation and activities focused on remaining abilities
why: Repeated testing can create distress without restoring lost memory.
Public correction may increase shame.
Performance comparisons may undermine enjoyable connection.
Strengths-based interaction supports dignity and meaningful contact.
takeaway: Promote connection rather than repeated memory testing in dementia.
learningObjective: Promote connection rather than repeated memory testing in dementia.

title: Evaluating a behaviour plan
stem: A dementia-care team changes bathing time and uses a familiar caregiver. Which outcomes should be tracked? Select all that apply.
options: Frequency and intensity of distress
Ability to participate comfortably in care
Staff agreement that the client should comply
Skin and hygiene needs being met
Whether every bath takes the identical number of minutes
why: Distress measures show whether the adaptation helps.
Participation reflects comfort and function.
Staff expectation alone is not a client outcome.
Essential physical-care outcomes remain relevant.
Identical timing is less important than individualized safe care.
takeaway: Evaluate dementia adaptations through distress, participation and physical needs.
learningObjective: Evaluate dementia adaptations through distress, participation and physical needs.

title: Delirium education for family
stem: A family says a client's fluctuating confusion means the client is choosing when to cooperate. What should the nurse explain?
options: Fluctuating attention can occur in delirium and needs clinical assessment
Inconsistency proves intentional behaviour
A lucid interval rules out acute illness
Memory exercises alone resolve the fluctuation
why: Fluctuation is a clinical feature rather than proof of motivation.
Intent cannot be inferred from variable attention.
Temporary clarity does not exclude delirium.
Underlying causes require assessment and appropriate treatment.
takeaway: Explain fluctuating attention without blaming the client.
learningObjective: Explain fluctuating attention without blaming the client.

title: Maintaining identity in dementia
stem: A former gardener with dementia is calmer when tending safe indoor plants. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace the activity with repeated orientation testing
Include the meaningful activity in the individualized care plan
Limit it to rewards for correct answers
Assume enjoyment means cognitive impairment has resolved
why: Testing may not provide the same connection or calming effect.
Familiar roles can support identity and wellbeing.
Meaningful activity should not depend on test performance.
Enjoyment and remaining skills coexist with dementia.
takeaway: Use meaningful familiar activities to support identity in dementia.
learningObjective: Use meaningful familiar activities to support identity in dementia.

title: Medical instability in restrictive eating
stem: A client restricting food reports fainting and has a slow pulse with low blood pressure. What is the priority?
options: Begin body-image journaling before further assessment
Discuss long-term meal preferences only
Arrange urgent physical assessment and coordinated eating-disorder care
Reassure based on the client's calm appearance
why: Reflection is secondary to possible physical instability.
Long-term planning does not address immediate risk.
Malnutrition can cause serious cardiovascular and electrolyte complications.
Calm behaviour does not establish physiologic stability.
takeaway: Prioritize physical instability in clients with restrictive eating.
learningObjective: Prioritize physical instability in clients with restrictive eating.

title: Weight and eating-disorder risk
stem: A client at an apparently average body size reports frequent vomiting after meals and palpitations. What should the nurse do?
options: Exclude an eating disorder because weight appears average
Recommend weight loss before further assessment
Focus only on whether clothing fits differently
Assess purging and possible medical complications promptly
why: Serious eating disorders can occur across body sizes.
Weight-loss advice may worsen the underlying problem.
Appearance does not assess electrolyte or cardiac risk.
Purging with palpitations requires timely clinical evaluation.
takeaway: Assess eating-disorder behaviour and complications independently of body size.
learningObjective: Assess eating-disorder behaviour and complications independently of body size.

title: Meal support in treatment
stem: A client receiving eating-disorder treatment becomes distressed before a planned meal. Which actions fit a coordinated nursing plan? Select all that apply.
options: Offer calm support using agreed coping strategies
Follow the team's consistent meal-support plan
Negotiate a new calorie target independently at each meal
Avoid comments praising thinness or judging appearance
Use peers' portion sizes to pressure the client
why: Coping support helps the client tolerate meal-related distress.
Consistency supports the established therapeutic approach.
Uncoordinated changes undermine the treatment plan.
Appearance comments can reinforce disordered beliefs or shame.
Comparison can intensify distress and competition.
takeaway: Provide consistent nonjudgmental meal support within the treatment plan.
learningObjective: Provide consistent nonjudgmental meal support within the treatment plan.

title: Refeeding monitoring
stem: A severely malnourished client begins prescribed nutritional rehabilitation. Why is close clinical monitoring necessary?
options: Intake recovery can produce important fluid and electrolyte shifts
Monitoring is needed only to verify willingness to eat
Weight alone detects every complication
Feeling hungry excludes medical risk
why: Refeeding can create potentially serious metabolic changes.
Physical monitoring is not a test of moral cooperation.
Weight does not describe electrolyte or cardiac status.
Appetite does not establish metabolic stability.
takeaway: Monitor physiologic response during nutritional rehabilitation.
learningObjective: Monitor physiologic response during nutritional rehabilitation.

title: Body-image statements during care
stem: A client receiving eating-disorder treatment asks, 'Do I look fat now?' What response best supports treatment?
options: Compare the client's body with other clients
Explore the anxiety and return to agreed health and coping goals
Provide repeated detailed weight reassurance
Ask family to judge the client's appearance
why: Comparison can reinforce disordered evaluation of bodies.
Addressing distress avoids making appearance the centre of care.
Reassurance cycles may maintain appearance checking.
External judging does not address the underlying fear.
takeaway: Respond to body-image anxiety without reinforcing appearance checking.
learningObjective: Respond to body-image anxiety without reinforcing appearance checking.

title: Binge eating and shame
stem: A client describes episodes of eating with loss of control and intense shame. What is the best nursing response?
options: Focus only on willpower and portion size
Recommend skipping the next day's meals
Assess the pattern, triggers, distress and need for specialist support
Compare the client's intake with the nurse's habits
why: Willpower framing oversimplifies the disorder and can increase shame.
Compensatory restriction may reinforce a harmful cycle.
Pattern assessment supports appropriate care without judgment.
Personal comparison does not assess the client's experience.
takeaway: Assess loss-of-control eating with a nonjudgmental clinical approach.
learningObjective: Assess loss-of-control eating with a nonjudgmental clinical approach.

title: Exercise despite nutritional instability
stem: A malnourished client continues exercising despite dizziness and a prescribed activity limit. What should the nurse do?
options: Praise exercise commitment as healthy behaviour
Negotiate a longer workout to preserve rapport
Ignore activity because it is usually beneficial
Address immediate symptoms and reinforce the coordinated activity plan
why: Exercise can be harmful in the context of current instability.
Unilateral negotiation may undermine a clinically necessary limit.
General exercise benefits do not override individual risk.
Physical safety and consistent treatment support are both needed.
takeaway: Judge exercise in the context of eating-disorder medical stability.
learningObjective: Judge exercise in the context of eating-disorder medical stability.

title: Eating-disorder recovery outcomes
stem: Which findings support meaningful progress in eating-disorder treatment? Select all that apply.
options: Improved ability to use coping skills around meals
More stable physical status under the treatment plan
Greater focus on comparing body size with others
Improved participation in valued activities
Less disclosure because symptoms feel shameful
why: Coping around meals supports functional recovery.
Physiologic stability is a central treatment outcome.
Increased comparison may reinforce disordered concerns.
Recovery includes life participation beyond food and weight.
Reduced disclosure may conceal worsening symptoms.
takeaway: Evaluate eating-disorder recovery through physical stability, coping and participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate eating-disorder recovery through physical stability, coping and participation.

title: Sensory distress in an autistic client
stem: An autistic adult becomes distressed by bright lights and several staff talking at once. What should the nurse do?
options: Reduce sensory demands and ask about preferred communication supports
Increase verbal prompting to improve cooperation
Interpret lack of eye contact as dishonesty
Continue the environment unchanged to encourage adaptation
why: Individual sensory and communication adjustments can reduce distress.
More prompting may intensify overload.
Eye contact is not a reliable measure of truthfulness.
Forced exposure is not a substitute for reasonable care adaptation.
takeaway: Adjust sensory and communication demands to the autistic client's needs.
learningObjective: Adjust sensory and communication demands to the autistic client's needs.

title: Communication without spoken language
stem: An autistic client uses a communication device and needs extra response time. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Direct every question only to the caregiver
Communicate with the client using their established system and allow time
Remove the device during assessment to reduce distraction
Assume speech absence means lack of understanding
why: The client's own communication remains central.
Familiar communication methods support participation and accurate assessment.
Removing the device can remove access to expression.
Speech ability does not determine comprehension or capacity.
takeaway: Preserve access to the client's established communication method.
learningObjective: Preserve access to the client's established communication method.

title: Unexpected routine change
stem: An autistic adolescent becomes overwhelmed when a planned examination order changes. What may help?
options: Provide repeated vague reassurance
Complete every step rapidly before further questions
Explain the revised sequence clearly and offer a visual or written plan
Treat distress as evidence the examination is unnecessary
why: Vague reassurance may not resolve uncertainty about what happens next.
Rushing may increase loss of control and overload.
A clear predictable sequence supports preparation and coping.
Distress calls for adaptation rather than an unsupported conclusion.
takeaway: Make changes predictable when routine disruption increases distress.
learningObjective: Make changes predictable when routine disruption increases distress.

title: Supporting attention during teaching
stem: A child with attention difficulties misses multistep instructions during a busy clinic visit. What is the best adaptation?
options: Repeat the same long explanation more loudly
Ask the caregiver to finish every task for the child
Interpret movement as proof the child is uninterested
Use brief steps, reduced distractions and active practice
why: Volume does not reduce working-memory demands.
Full takeover removes appropriate learning opportunities.
Movement does not establish lack of motivation.
Task simplification and practice fit the observed attention needs.
takeaway: Adapt teaching to attention and working-memory capacity.
learningObjective: Adapt teaching to attention and working-memory capacity.

title: Escalating sensory overload
stem: Which observations suggest an individualized sensory-support plan needs adjustment? Select all that apply.
options: Distress consistently rises during overlapping staff conversations
The client requests a quieter waiting area
The client uses a familiar communication aid successfully
Care becomes difficult after unexpected physical contact
The client selects a preferred calming activity
why: A repeated trigger identifies an environmental demand to reduce.
A direct request identifies a potentially useful accommodation.
Effective communication access supports rather than undermines the plan.
Unexpected touch can be a modifiable source of overload.
Chosen calming activity can be an effective existing support.
takeaway: Use the client's responses to refine sensory accommodations.
learningObjective: Use the client's responses to refine sensory accommodations.

title: Consistent boundaries across staff
stem: A client asks one nurse to make an exception another nurse declined under the agreed care plan. What should the nurse do?
options: Clarify the need and respond consistently with the team plan
Grant the exception to show greater understanding
Criticize the other nurse in front of the client
Refuse discussion because the request was asked before
why: Consistency with respectful assessment supports predictable care.
Uncoordinated exceptions can create confusion and conflict.
Staff criticism undermines the therapeutic team.
The client's concern can be heard even when limits remain.
takeaway: Combine consistent boundaries with respectful exploration of the need.
learningObjective: Combine consistent boundaries with respectful exploration of the need.

title: Fear of abandonment after a schedule change
stem: A client says a nurse's planned absence proves nobody cares. What is the most therapeutic response?
options: Promise never to be absent again
Acknowledge the feeling and explain the continuity plan clearly
Ask the client to earn extra attention through compliance
Avoid future discussion of staffing changes
why: An impossible promise undermines reliable boundaries.
Validation and predictability address distress without unrealistic assurances.
Conditional attention can distort the therapeutic relationship.
Avoidance can increase uncertainty and mistrust.
takeaway: Address abandonment fears with validation and predictable continuity.
learningObjective: Address abandonment fears with validation and predictable continuity.

title: Requests for personal social contact
stem: A client nearing discharge asks to connect with the nurse's personal social-media account. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept because the clinical relationship is nearly over
Offer another staff member's personal account
Explain the boundary and review appropriate ongoing support contacts
Ignore the request and end the conversation abruptly
why: Discharge does not automatically remove professional boundary obligations.
Another personal account does not resolve the boundary concern.
A respectful limit preserves professionalism and continuity of support.
Abrupt avoidance misses an opportunity to explain and support transition.
takeaway: Redirect personal-contact requests toward appropriate continuing supports.
learningObjective: Redirect personal-contact requests toward appropriate continuing supports.

title: Anger after a limit
stem: A client raises their voice when a previously agreed boundary is maintained. No immediate physical threat is present. What should the nurse do?
options: Match the client's volume to demonstrate authority
Withdraw every planned support as a consequence
Repeatedly renegotiate the boundary during peak distress
Acknowledge frustration and restate the limit with a feasible alternative
why: Escalating volume can intensify conflict.
Broad withdrawal of care is not a therapeutic response.
Repeated negotiation may undermine clarity during heightened emotion.
Calm consistency with an alternative supports regulation and predictability.
takeaway: Maintain boundaries calmly while offering acceptable alternatives.
learningObjective: Maintain boundaries calmly while offering acceptable alternatives.

title: Reflecting on strong reactions
stem: A nurse feels unusually irritated by a client's repeated requests. Which actions support therapeutic care? Select all that apply.
options: Reflect on personal reactions and possible bias
Seek appropriate supervision or team consultation
Use irritation as evidence the client intends manipulation
Continue objective assessment of the client's needs
Ask the client to reassure the nurse about their performance
why: Self-awareness helps prevent personal reactions from driving care.
Consultation can support consistent safe responses.
Emotional reactions do not establish the client's intent.
Assessment should remain grounded in observable needs and behaviour.
The client should not be tasked with meeting the nurse's emotional needs.
takeaway: Use reflection and consultation when personal reactions affect care.
learningObjective: Use reflection and consultation when personal reactions affect care.

title: Spiritual distress after diagnosis
stem: A client says, 'My illness means I am being punished.' What should the nurse do?
options: Explore the meaning and ask whether spiritual support would help
Confirm the explanation to respect religion
Debate the client's beliefs immediately
Arrange a religious representative without asking preference
why: Open exploration respects meaning while assessing distress and desired support.
Respect does not require affirming a harmful interpretation.
Debate may undermine trust and shut down discussion.
Spiritual support should reflect the client's wishes.
takeaway: Explore spiritual distress without imposing or confirming an explanation.
learningObjective: Explore spiritual distress without imposing or confirming an explanation.

title: A request for prayer
stem: A client asks for spiritual support before a difficult procedure. The nurse does not share the belief. What is the best response?
options: Suggest waiting for family to lead prayer after the procedure
Ask what support is desired and facilitate an appropriate resource
Offer a relaxation exercise as a replacement for spiritual support
Ask the nearest available visitor to pray with the client
why: Family support may be welcome, but waiting may not address the client's present request.
Client-defined assistance respects spiritual needs and professional boundaries.
Relaxation can complement care but should not automatically replace the requested spiritual support.
An unfamiliar visitor may not match the client's beliefs, consent or privacy needs.
takeaway: Facilitate spiritual support according to the client's wishes.
learningObjective: Facilitate spiritual support according to the client's wishes.

title: Moral distress in a family caregiver
stem: A caregiver says, 'Accepting respite means I have failed my parent.' What response best supports reflection?
options: Agree that dedicated relatives never need breaks
Tell the caregiver guilt is irrational
Explore what good caregiving means and how rest supports sustainable care
Choose respite dates before discussing the concern
why: Unrealistic expectations can worsen exhaustion and guilt.
Dismissal does not address the caregiver's values.
Exploring meaning can connect respite with continued caring rather than failure.
Imposed arrangements may bypass the barrier to accepting help.
takeaway: Explore caregiving values when guilt prevents needed support.
learningObjective: Explore caregiving values when guilt prevents needed support.

title: Evaluating crisis resolution
stem: After an acute situational crisis, a client appears calmer but still cannot identify a safe place to stay tonight. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: End the interview because visible distress improved
Give general relaxation advice only
Assume family accommodation without checking
Clarify immediate shelter, safety and follow-up arrangements
why: Reduced visible emotion does not establish that practical risk has resolved.
Relaxation does not provide safe accommodation.
Available support must be confirmed rather than assumed.
Crisis resolution requires an actionable plan for immediate needs.
takeaway: Evaluate crisis recovery through practical safety and coping, not appearance alone.
learningObjective: Evaluate crisis recovery through practical safety and coping, not appearance alone.

title: A client-defined support network
stem: Which actions help create a useful psychosocial support plan? Select all that apply.
options: Ask whom the client considers supportive
Clarify what each willing support person can realistically do
Assume biological relatives must be the main supports
Include professional or community options for unmet needs
Share details with every named person before obtaining agreement
why: Support networks may include friends, partners or chosen family.
Specific feasible roles make the plan operational.
Family structure does not determine who provides effective support.
Formal resources can address gaps informal supports cannot meet.
Naming someone does not automatically authorize all information sharing.
takeaway: Build support plans from the client's relationships, consent and realistic resources.
learningObjective: Build support plans from the client's relationships, consent and realistic resources.

title: Relocation and continuity of identity
stem: An older adult newly admitted to assisted living withdraws from meals and says nothing feels familiar. No acute illness is identified. What should the nurse do?
options: Begin a structured orientation test at every meal
Explore familiar routines and meaningful belongings to support adjustment
Require participation in the busiest group activity
Tell family to reduce visits so independence develops
why: Repeated testing may not address the emotional loss of familiarity.
Personal routines and meaningful objects can support continuity and a sense of belonging.
A busy activity may overwhelm rather than help a withdrawn new resident.
Supportive contact can assist adjustment and should not be restricted by assumption.
takeaway: Preserve familiar routines and identity during a major living transition.
learningObjective: Preserve familiar routines and identity during a major living transition.
